The Numbers Behind A Missed Opportunity

Puno recorded more than 3,000 visitors during the Semana Santa 2025 long holiday. That figure confirms steady demand for the altiplano destination, home to Lake Titicaca and a rich living culture.

Yet regional data shows overall tourism grew just 3% to 4% during the 2025 high season. For a region that anchors the classic Cusco–Puno–Arequipa corridor, that pace leaves considerable economic value on the table.

Why Puno Tourism Stalls Despite Strong Demand

The bottleneck starts with promotion. Regional authorities have been slow to build a coherent marketing strategy, leaving Puno with limited digital visibility and few partnerships with international tour operators.

Without consistent branding and sales channels abroad, the destination relies heavily on domestic travellers and backpackers. That narrow base cannot sustain the kind of growth seen in Cusco or Arequipa.

Roads And Runways: The Infrastructure Deficit

Much of Puno’s regional road network remains unpaved, making overland travel slow and expensive. Tour operators report that poor road conditions push up vehicle maintenance costs and discourage multi-day itineraries.

Air access tells a similar story. Flights into Inca Manco Cápac International Airport in Juliaca are infrequent and carry high fares, effectively capping the number of foreign visitors who can reach the region comfortably.

The Cusco–Puno–Arequipa Corridor Loses Competitiveness

The three-city circuit is one of Peru’s most iconic travel routes. But when Puno becomes the hardest leg to reach and navigate, tour operators shorten itineraries or skip the altiplano altogether.

Missing signage, scarce tourist information offices, and incomplete terminal facilities compound the problem. Each friction point nudges travellers toward easier alternatives elsewhere in southern Peru.

Environmental Stress And Informality Add Risk

Lake Titicaca itself faces growing environmental pressure, including contamination that worries both visitors and conservation groups. An informal tourism sector further erodes service quality and tax collection.

For investors and expats eyeing Peru’s hospitality market, these factors raise the risk profile of Puno-based projects. The fundamentals are strong, but the enabling environment remains weak.

What The Data Means For Investors And Expats

Puno’s 3-4% growth rate signals a market that is moving, but slowly. For hospitality investors, the gap between current performance and potential represents a long-term opportunity tied to infrastructure upgrades.

Expats living in Arequipa or Cusco already use Puno as a weekend and holiday destination. Better roads and more reliable air links would deepen that integration and lift property values across the corridor.

What To Watch Next

Regional authorities have signalled interest in public-private partnerships to upgrade road segments and improve tourist facilities. Any concrete tender announcements would be a leading indicator for the sector.

Watch also for airline route decisions. A new carrier or increased frequency into Juliaca would immediately shift the arrival numbers and signal market confidence in the altiplano.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Puno tourism stall during long holidays despite strong demand?

Puno tourism stalls primarily because of weak promotional strategies and poor infrastructure. Unpaved roads, expensive and infrequent flights to Juliaca, and limited digital marketing keep visitor numbers far below the region’s potential, even during peak holiday periods like Semana Santa.

How does poor infrastructure affect the Cusco–Puno–Arequipa travel corridor?

Poor road conditions and costly air access make Puno the weakest link in the corridor. Tour operators often shorten or skip the Puno leg, redirecting travellers to destinations with better connectivity and services, which reduces overall revenue for the altiplano region.

What would it take to unlock Puno’s tourism potential?

Unlocking Puno’s potential requires coordinated investment in paved roads, more frequent and affordable flights, a professional destination-marketing campaign, and upgraded tourist facilities. Public-private partnerships and regional government tenders are the mechanisms to watch for early signs of change.

World.title: Mexico City’s Zócalo Hosts Free Indigenous Cultures Festival

Cultural Tourism

Key Facts —Dates. The festival runs from 7 to 23 August 2026, open daily. —Location. The Zócalo, Mexico City’s main square, hosts the entire event. —Hours. Activities run from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. every day. —Admission. Entry is free; food and crafts are sold at varying prices. —Offerings. Traditional food, live music, dance, textiles and workshops are featured.

Mexico City has confirmed the 2026 Indigenous Cultures Festival will return to the Zócalo from 7 to 23 August, bringing seventeen days of food, music and crafts to one of Latin America’s most iconic public squares.

A Flagship Event Returns to the Zócalo

The Fiesta de las Culturas Indígenas, Pueblos y Barrios Originarios de la Ciudad de México will once again transform the Plaza de la Constitución into a living showcase of native traditions. Organisers have set the 2026 edition for 7 to 23 August, with gates open from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. every day, including weekends.

Admission remains free, a deliberate choice by city authorities to keep the event accessible to residents and international visitors alike. The Zócalo, one of the largest public squares in the world, provides a fitting stage for an event that draws hundreds of thousands of attendees each year.

What Visitors Can Expect at the Indigenous Cultures Festival

The festival brings together indigenous communities from across Mexico City’s original neighbourhoods and from other regions of the country. Stalls and stages fill the square, offering a dense programme of gastronomy, live performance and artisanal trade.

Traditional food is the anchor: visitors can sample dishes prepared by cooks from Nahua, Mixtec, Mazahua, Otomí and other communities. Handicrafts, textiles, herbal medicine and workshops on native languages and cosmovision round out the daily schedule, alongside music and dance performances that run well into the evening.

The Economic Read-Through for Mexico City

Cultural tourism is a growing line item in Mexico City’s economy, and the Indigenous Cultures Festival is one of its highest-volume free events. Hotels, restaurants and transport operators in the Centro Histórico see a measurable uptick during the seventeen-day run, with foot traffic spilling into surrounding streets and commercial corridors.

For artisans and food vendors, the festival is a direct-to-consumer marketplace with no intermediary costs beyond their stall fees. Many participants report that sales during the event represent a significant share of their annual income, making the festival as much an economic development tool as a cultural showcase.

What the Festival Signals for Investors and Expats

The continuity of large-scale public events in the Zócalo signals a city government committed to keeping the historic core active and internationally visible. For investors in hospitality, retail and food-and-beverage, the festival calendar provides a predictable demand spike worth planning around.

Expats and long-stay visitors get a concentrated introduction to Mexico’s indigenous cultural landscape without leaving the capital. The festival’s free admission and central location make it a low-barrier entry point for anyone looking to understand the country beyond the usual tourist circuits.

Planning a Visit: Practical Considerations

The Zócalo is served by Metro stations Zócalo/Tenochtitlán (Line 2) and Allende (Line 2), with multiple Metrobús and bus routes stopping nearby. August falls within Mexico City’s rainy season, so afternoons often bring brief but heavy showers; visitors should pack accordingly.

While entry is free, food and craft purchases are cash-based in many stalls, though card acceptance has grown in recent years. Arriving early in the day offers a calmer experience, while evenings bring larger crowds and the most ambitious music programming.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the 2026 Indigenous Cultures Festival in Mexico City?

The festival runs from 7 to 23 August 2026, every day from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. It takes place at the Zócalo, Mexico City’s main square, and admission is free.

What can I buy and eat at the festival?

Visitors can purchase traditional dishes prepared by indigenous cooks, as well as handicrafts, textiles, herbal remedies and art. Food and craft prices vary by vendor, and many stalls operate on a cash basis.

Is the festival suitable for international visitors and families?

Yes, the event is designed to be broadly accessible, with free entry, a central location and programming that appeals to all ages. Workshops, music and dance performances run throughout the day, and the square is easily reached by public transport.

World.title: Colombia’s Bocas De Ceniza River Mouth Gets Tourist Revival
World.content:
Colombia · Infrastructure & Tourism

Key Facts —Location. Bocas de Ceniza is the main mouth of the Magdalena River where it meets the Caribbean Sea in northern Barranquilla. —The Project. A public investment is restoring the western breakwater and building a new waterfront promenade, viewpoint, and electric tourist train route. —Sustainable Mobility. The plan includes 2.6 km of rail line, 2.2 km of cycle path, and 2.6 km of pedestrian path connecting Las Flores to the river mouth. —Economic Goals. Authorities aim to generate local employment, boost commerce, and position the site as a flagship Caribbean coast attraction. —Current Status. Works are underway with 1.5 km of the breakwater already rehabilitated, though no official opening date has been published.

Bocas de Ceniza, the dramatic point where the Magdalena River pushes into the Caribbean Sea, is being transformed from a rustic local spot into a modern tourist corridor that Barranquilla hopes will attract visitors and investment to Colombia’s northern coast.

Barranquilla Turns Bocas de Ceniza Into a Tourist Draw (Photo internet reproduction)

A Natural Spectacle Gets a Modern Makeover

For decades, reaching Bocas de Ceniza meant a bumpy ride on an artisanal train or the back of a motorcycle along crumbling breakwaters. The journey was part of the adventure, but the infrastructure was never designed for mass tourism.

That is now changing under a coordinated push by Barranquilla’s district government and national authorities. The plan reimagines the entire corridor from the Las Flores neighbourhood to the river mouth as a seamless waterfront experience spanning nearly three kilometres.

The project’s centrepiece is the restoration of the Tajamar Occidental, the western breakwater that guides visitors to the point where brown river water collides with blue sea. Officials report that 1.5 kilometres have already been intervened, with surface levelling and adaptation work to improve safety for fishermen, residents, and tourists alike.

The Electric Train and the New Waterfront Corridor

Perhaps the most visible change for returning visitors will be the replacement of the old artisanal train with a new electric tourist tram. The route restores the traditional connection between Las Flores, Puerto Mocho beach, and the Tajamar Occidental.

The mobility package is substantial: 2.6 kilometres of rail line, 2.2 kilometres of cycle path, and 2.6 kilometres of pedestrian walkway. Two stations, at Las Flores and Puerto Mocho, are already in their finishing stages and will include ticket offices, information points, kitchens, and commercial stands.

Mayor Alejandro Char has promised the renewed corridor will be fully accessible to electric motorcycles, bicycles, skaters, runners, and pedestrians. The goal is a continuous, car-free waterfront experience hugging the Magdalena River, the Mallorquín marsh, and mangroves all the way to the sea.

A Viewpoint and a Monument at the River’s Mouth

At the tip of the breakwater, where visitors currently scramble over rocks for a view, the city is preparing a proper tourism infrastructure. Plans include a pedestrian path and a viewing platform crowned with a monumental monolith.

Local media have described the new malecón and mirador as a “new tourist jewel” for Barranquilla. The design aims to consolidate the corridor along the river’s edge while enabling ecological recovery of the surrounding landscape.

The sensory experience of the river meeting the sea remains the star attraction. But the new infrastructure promises to make that experience safer, more comfortable, and accessible to a far broader range of visitors than the rustic access of years past.

The Business Case for Bocas de Ceniza

For investors and business owners watching Colombia’s Caribbean coast, the Bocas de Ceniza project signals a broader municipal strategy to diversify Barranquilla’s economy beyond its traditional port and industrial base. Tourism infrastructure is a long-term bet on visitor spending and real estate value along the northern corridor.

The project explicitly targets employment generation and local commerce. Revitalising the train and waterfront responds to years of resident demand for improved infrastructure, while the new commercial stands at the tram stations create small-business opportunities in Las Flores and Puerto Mocho.

The environmental angle also carries weight with international development partners and eco-conscious travellers. The works tie into broader efforts around the Ciénaga de Mallorquín, a coastal wetland, aiming to balance ecological restoration with controlled, sustainable tourism.

What Visitors and Expats Should Know Now

As of the latest reports, works are actively underway but no official opening date has been published for the full corridor or the new mirador. Authorities state repeatedly that the electric train and waterfront route will be operational “prontamente,” though Colombian infrastructure timelines often reward patience.

In the interim, Bocas de Ceniza remains accessible as a natural attraction. Artisanal train services and motorcycle rides still operate on some segments, though conditions can be rustic and variable depending on weather and ongoing construction.

For expats based in Barranquilla or considering a move to Colombia’s Caribbean coast, the project adds another recreational asset to a city that has invested heavily in public spaces over the past decade. The Gran Malecón along the Magdalena has already proven the model; Bocas de Ceniza extends it to the sea.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Bocas de Ceniza and why is it significant?

Bocas de Ceniza is the main mouth of the Magdalena River where it flows into the Caribbean Sea, located in the Las Flores area of northern Barranquilla. It is a striking natural spectacle where brown river water meets blue ocean, and it has long been a local attraction accessed by artisanal train or motorcycle along the breakwaters.

When will the new Bocas de Ceniza tourist corridor open?

Authorities have not published an exact opening date, though works are underway with 1.5 kilometres of the western breakwater already rehabilitated and the electric train stations in finishing phases. Officials say the corridor will be operational soon, but visitors should check local updates before planning a trip around the new infrastructure.

How do I visit Bocas de Ceniza while construction is ongoing?

Bocas de Ceniza remains accessible as a natural attraction during the construction period. Artisanal train services and motorcycle rides still operate on some segments, though conditions can be rustic and variable.

Visitors should expect ongoing works and plan accordingly, especially during the rainy season when access may be more challenging.

The inaugural exhibition opens Wednesday, July 29, at the Palomar del Príncipe in La Candelaria. —First Feature. The debut show highlights architect Julio Enrique López’s drawings and historical notes on the city. —Public Access. Entry is free, with visiting hours Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. —City Initiative. Bogotá architectural history takes the spotlight as the District Institute of Cultural Heritage launches a free, permanent exhibition cycle in La Candelaria, deepening the city’s cultural offer for residents and visitors alike.

A New Window into Bogotá Architectural History

The District Institute of Cultural Heritage (IDPC) has unveiled “Architectures of Heritage,” a new permanent exhibition cycle. It is designed to document and celebrate the evolution of the capital’s built environment.

The programme launches on Wednesday, July 29, at the Palomar del Príncipe, a historic venue in the heart of La Candelaria. Admission is free, making it an accessible cultural anchor for the city’s most storied neighbourhood.

The IDPC positions the cycle as a multidisciplinary platform. It will showcase the work of architects, researchers, illustrators, and other creators who interpret Bogotá’s urban fabric.

Julio Enrique López: Drawing the City’s Memory

The inaugural exhibition is dedicated to architect Julio Enrique López. His detailed drawings serve as a visual archive of Bogotá’s architectural heritage.

The show pairs López’s illustrations with historical notes he authored. Together, they contextualise the social and architectural evolution of the places he depicted.

Organisers describe his work as a key tool for observing and communicating heritage. It offers visitors a direct, intimate look at how the city’s streetscapes have transformed over decades.

La Candelaria as a Cultural Anchor

The choice of the Palomar del Príncipe reinforces La Candelaria’s role as Bogotá’s cultural and historical core. The colonial-era building itself is a piece of the story the exhibition aims to tell.

The venue sits on Calle 12b No. 2-96, within walking distance of the Plaza de Bolívar and the city’s top museums.

Its central location makes the exhibition a natural stop on any heritage walking tour.

For expats and long-stay visitors, the permanent nature of the cycle adds a reliable, repeatable cultural fixture. It strengthens the neighbourhood’s appeal as a liveable, walkable district with deep historical roots.

The “Bogotá, mi Ciudad, mi Casa” Framework

“Architectures of Heritage” operates under the city initiative “Bogotá, mi Ciudad, mi Casa.” This programme aims to strengthen residents’ connection to their urban environment through cultural and educational projects.

The framework signals a sustained public investment in heritage education. It aligns with broader efforts to position Bogotá as a competitive destination for cultural tourism in Latin America.

For investors tracking urban development, such initiatives often correlate with property value stabilisation in historic districts. They signal municipal commitment to preserving the character that draws boutique hotels, restaurants, and creative enterprises.

Practical Details and What to Watch Next

The exhibition is open Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with no entry fee. The IDPC’s Documentation Center will house the cycle permanently, rotating featured creators over time.

Visitors can expect future instalments to highlight different disciplines and periods of Bogotá architectural history. The IDPC has indicated the programme will continuously incorporate new research and artistic perspectives.

The launch adds a fresh layer to Bogotá’s cultural calendar at a time when the city is working to attract more remote workers and long-term visitors. It is a small but telling piece of a larger strategy to sell the city not just as a business hub, but as a place with a soul worth exploring.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the “Architectures of Heritage” exhibition cycle?

It is a new permanent exhibition programme launched by Bogotá’s District Institute of Cultural Heritage (IDPC). The cycle focuses on the city’s architectural and urban history through the work of architects, illustrators, and researchers.

The first exhibition features drawings and historical notes by architect Julio Enrique López.

Where and when can I visit the inaugural exhibition in Bogotá?

The exhibition opens on Wednesday, July 29, at the Palomar del Príncipe, located at Calle 12b No. 2-96 in the La Candelaria neighbourhood.

It is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and admission is completely free.

Is there a cost to enter the IDPC’s heritage exhibition?

No, entry is free for all visitors. The exhibition is part of the public initiative “Bogotá, mi Ciudad, mi Casa,” designed to make the city’s cultural and architectural heritage accessible to everyone.

World.title: Panama Tops Best Country for Expats Ranking 3rd Year
World.content:
Frontier Living & Investment

Key Facts —Global number one. InterNations surveys rank Panama as the top country worldwide for expats in 2026 for the third consecutive year. —Dollarized stability. Panama uses the US dollar as its official currency, eliminating exchange-rate risk for expats earning in dollars. —Cost advantage. Panama City is roughly 40% cheaper than London and 48% less expensive than New York, excluding rent. —Accessible residency. The Pensionado and Friendly Nations Visa programmes offer straightforward paths to residency for retirees and professionals. —Monthly budget. A single person can live comfortably in Panama City on $1,100 to $1,800 per month, while a couple needs roughly $2,000 to $3,000.

Panama has cemented its position at the very top of the best countries for expats in 2026, with Panama City offering a rare combination of dollarized economic stability, modern infrastructure, and a cost of living that undercuts major Western cities by nearly half.

Panama tops the InterNations Expat Insider ranking for a third consecutive year. (Photo internet reproduction)

Why Panama Tops the Global Expat Rankings

For the third consecutive year, Panama has claimed the number-one spot in InterNations surveys measuring expat satisfaction across the globe. The country was the only one to rank first across all five indices: working abroad, basic essentials, ease of settling in, personal finances, and quality of life.

This is not a marginal victory. Panama outpaces Mexico, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, and Brazil in the same survey, while traditional European favourites like Spain, Portugal, and Luxembourg trail behind.

The distinction matters because different rankings measure different things. Broader immigration indices that weigh welfare-state benefits and labour-market regulation place Switzerland, Iceland, and Australia at the top.

Panama sits at position 51 in those metrics, which tells a clear story: the country excels at the lived daily experience of being a foreigner, not at replicating a European social model.

Panama City: A Modern Capital Built for International Living

Panama City is the undisputed hub of the country’s expat appeal. The Global Liveability Index 2024 scored it at 75 out of 100, placing it among Latin America’s most liveable capitals.

The skyline tells part of the story: a forest of glass towers overlooking the Pacific, housing more than 100 international banks, regional headquarters for multinationals, and a financial district that functions entirely in dollars. Tocumen International Airport serves as a regional hub, offering direct flights to the Americas and Europe that make the city a practical base for frequent travellers.

Private healthcare is a major draw. Hospitals in the capital operate to international standards, with English-speaking staff and equipment comparable to facilities in the United States or Europe.

International schools and bilingual programmes make the city viable for families, while a growing cultural scene of restaurants, galleries, and events keeps pace with the influx of foreign residents.

The Real Cost of Living in Panama City

Panama City is not cheap by Latin American standards, but it is sharply discounted when measured against the cities most expats leave behind. Numbeo data shows the capital is roughly 40% cheaper than London and 48% less expensive than New York, excluding rent.

A single person can live comfortably on $1,100 to $1,800 per month without extravagance. For a couple, local forums and expat guides point to $2,000 to $3,000 monthly as a reasonable range for a central apartment, groceries, transport, and dining out.

Housing is the largest variable. A one-bedroom furnished apartment in prime expat neighbourhoods such as Punta Pacífica, San Francisco, or Costa del Este typically rents for $850 to $1,500 per month.

Moving to the outskirts or to smaller cities like Boquete can bring rents down to around $400, though at the cost of urban convenience.

Neighbourhoods Where Expats Settle

Casco Viejo, the city’s restored colonial quarter, attracts those seeking character, nightlife, and a walkable streetscape. It is the most popular neighbourhood for younger expats and digital nomads who value atmosphere over square footage.

El Cangrejo offers a more relaxed urban feel, with tree-lined streets, restaurants, and a mix of professionals and students. San Francisco is a rising residential zone with a broad range of housing options and good access to services.

For those with larger budgets, Punta Paitilla, Punta Pacífica, and Costa del Este deliver high-rise living with ocean views, modern amenities, and concentrations of foreign residents. Marbella and Obarrio round out the list of central districts with strong expat presence and easy access to the financial core.

Visa Pathways That Make the Move Practical

Panama’s residency programmes are a cornerstone of its expat appeal. The Pensionado Visa, widely regarded as one of the world’s most generous retirement programmes, requires a minimum monthly pension of around $1,000 and unlocks significant discounts on medical bills, utilities, travel, and entertainment.

The Friendly Nations Visa targets professionals and entrepreneurs from a list of designated countries, offering a path to residency and eventual citizenship. Both programmes are notably more accessible than comparable schemes in Europe or North America, with processing times that expats consistently describe as manageable.

Foreign-sourced income is not taxed, a policy that resonates with digital nomads, remote workers, and retirees drawing pensions or investment income from abroad. Combined with the dollarized economy, this creates a financial environment that is both stable and predictable.

How Panama Compares to Other Best Countries for Expats

The global expat landscape in 2026 splits into two broad categories. Switzerland, Iceland, Australia, and Germany lead on institutional strength: high salaries, robust public services, and deep social safety nets.

The trade-offs are demanding visa processes, very high costs, and in several cases, cold climates and language barriers.

Panama, Mexico, Portugal, and Thailand lead on lived expat experience: easier integration, large international communities, lower costs, and favourable climates. The trade-offs here include less comprehensive public institutions and the need to choose your city and neighbourhood carefully to match your expectations.

Panama City occupies a unique middle ground. It delivers urban sophistication and financial infrastructure that rival global cities, at a cost closer to mid-tier Latin American capitals.

For someone seeking a new life abroad without sacrificing modern comforts or paying London or New York prices, it is arguably the most balanced option on the 2026 map.

What to Watch Before You Commit

The tropical climate is a genuine adjustment. Temperatures range from 24 to 35 degrees Celsius year-round with high humidity, and not everyone adapts comfortably.

Housing costs in the most desirable central neighbourhoods have risen steadily, and budgeting realistically for rent is essential.

Panama’s institutional framework is not Northern Europe. Public services, bureaucracy, and infrastructure outside the capital can be inconsistent.

The country’s strength lies in what it offers to those who arrive with independent means or remote income, not in replicating a welfare state.

For investors and professionals watching Latin America, Panama City represents a stable, dollar-denominated entry point with a proven track record of attracting and retaining foreign residents. The InterNations data confirms what the skyline suggests: this is where the world’s expats are choosing to build their next chapter.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Panama really the best country for expats in 2026?

Yes, according to InterNations surveys of expatriates worldwide, Panama ranks number one for the third consecutive year. It scored first across all five measured categories: working abroad, basic essentials, ease of settling in, personal finances, and quality of life.

Broader immigration indices that weigh welfare-state benefits place European countries higher, but for day-to-day expat experience, Panama leads.

How much money do I need to live comfortably in Panama City?

A single person can live comfortably on $1,100 to $1,800 per month, while a couple typically needs $2,000 to $3,000 monthly. A one-bedroom furnished apartment in a central expat neighbourhood rents for $850 to $1,500.

Panama City is roughly 40% cheaper than London and 48% less expensive than New York, excluding rent.

What visas are available for expats moving to Panama?

The two most popular pathways are the Pensionado Visa, which requires a minimum monthly pension of around $1,000 and offers significant discounts on services, and the Friendly Nations Visa, which allows professionals and entrepreneurs from designated countries to obtain residency and eventually citizenship. Foreign-sourced income is not taxed in Panama.

World.title: Frida Kahlo’s Personal Items Debut in Buenos Aires at Malba
World.content:
LIFE: Buenos Aires

Key Facts —Exhibition. “Viva Frida” runs from 18 September 2026 to 14 March 2027 at Malba in Buenos Aires. —First. It marks the first time Frida Kahlo’s personal objects from Casa Azul are shown in South America. —Scale. The show features 365 objects, making it the most complete version of this travelling project to date. —Collection. Items include Tehuana dresses, orthopaedic corsets, jewellery, cosmetics, diaries, and letters. —Context. The exhibition is the grand finale of Malba’s 25th-anniversary celebrations.

The Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires (Malba) will host the most comprehensive Frida Kahlo exhibition ever staged in South America, bringing the iconic artist’s personal belongings from Mexico City’s Casa Azul to Argentina for the first time.

Viva Frida opens at Malba in Buenos Aires on 19 September 2026. (Photo internet reproduction)
