World.title: The French presidential candidate who wants to blow up the Franco-German engine
World.content:
Instead, Mélenchon wants France to strengthen ties with China as well as French-speaking countries in Africa, as well as South American countries. He sees the United States as an imperialist danger, while Germany — despite its turbulent relations with President Donald Trump — views the transatlantic relationship as paramount to its foreign policy. Mélenchon is opposed to Germany’s deeply held attachment to its free-market economic model and favors a planned economy instead.

Mélenchon is also critical of Germany’s rearmament and the continued presence of U.S. nuclear weapons on its soil, which he said: “raise serious security concerns for neighboring countries.” Berlin aims to become Europe’s predominant military power in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and American retrenchment from Europe.

Mélenchon’s 2015 book “Bismarck’s Herring,” subtitled “The German Poison,” was meant to be a response to the many politicians who at the time in France viewed Germany as a policy model thanks to its low unemployment and strong growth rates.

Mélenchon pointed to the poverty rate in Germany, which at that time was several points higher than in France, and low birth rates as examples of the model’s failures.

“My goal is to pierce through the veil of bliss surrounding so many commentators who are fascinated by Germany,” reads the book’s blurb. “A monster has been born right before our eyes — the child of deregulated finance and a country that has devoted itself to it, ravaged by the accelerated aging of its population.”

Parts of French media, even left-leaning outlet Libération, deemed the book excessively Germanophobic. In it, Mélenchon adopts a provocative tone and states that “political confrontation with German governments is one of the conditions for the liberation of peoples.”

World.title: As France burns, the far right sees an opening
World.content:
“All the proposals that we have been putting forward for years with Marine and Jordan [Bardella] … today we realize that those are the only ones that could have spared us these situations, from protecting us from wildfires to saving our children,” she said. “Current events, alas, prove us right.”

Whether that argument will gain traction remains uncertain. But National Rally may not need voters to see it as an authority on climate change; its opening lies instead in the declining credibility of the parties that have governed France — and a sense among some voters that the state is no longer capable of protecting them.

Recent research shared with POLITICO — based on four focus groups with former center and center-left voters who appeared unlikely to support those parties again — found repeated references to a country that was falling apart. Participants cited a series of recent crises, including the murder of an 11-year-old girl by a suspect previously known to police, as evidence that the government was failing to act.

Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella arrive to attend a ceremony in Nice, France on July 14, 2026. | Pool photo by Philippe Magoni via AFP/Getty Images

That frustration extends to climate preparedness. In a YouGov poll published this month, 74 percent of respondents said they were dissatisfied with Macron’s climate-adaptation policies.

“The National Rally mechanically benefits from its anti-system positioning whenever there is a news event that gives the impression, right or wrong, that successive governments have not taken effective action to address the difficulties faced by the French people,” said Mathieu Gallard, research director at Ipsos France, a polling firm.

The fires have burned more than 1,000 square kilometers across southwestern France since the start of the summer — an area roughly 10 times the size of Paris — and forced more than 200,000 people from their homes. Coming after an extreme heatwave left the countryside tinder-dry, they have already scorched nearly twice as much land as during the last devastating fire season in 2022.

World.title: What voters really think of Andy Burnham
World.content:
While there are still as many as three years to go before the next general election is called, Burnham’s arrival in No. 10 Downing Street — on the initial showing at least — seems to have changed the picture dramatically. Several pollsters in recent days have given Labour a small lead over Reform for the first time since the spring of 2025.

The POLITICO Poll delves deeper into voters’ first impressions of the new prime minister.

More than half the public — 54 percent — watched Burnham’s first speech on the steps of Downing Street after becoming prime minister, in which he set out his initial priorities for the job — and they gave him rave reviews.

Majorities agreed that he set out a clear vision for the country, that he’ll do the things he promised, and that he understands the problems that people like them face. He delivered the speech without notes or a lectern and voters seem to have approved of his communication style: Most said he is a good public speaker and his speech made them “feel more hopeful about the future” — a potentially significant mood shift, especially as Burnham promised to “bring back hope.”

That seems to have helped the new prime minister to make inroads among Reform voters — some of whom are former Labour voters the party hopes to win back.

Some 60 percent of Reform voters who watched Burnham’s first speech said they thought he was “a good public speaker.” One in three trusted that he would “do the things he promised” and said his speech made them feel more hopeful about the future. An even higher number — 44 percent — said Burnham “understands the problems facing people like me.” That’s more than the 38 percent of Reform voters who saw the speech and thought Burnham did not understand their problems.

World.title: EU pitches Brexit reset tuition fees compromise
World.content:
The EU has been pushing for European students to pay domestic rate tuition fees when studying at British universities, as they did before Brexit.

At £9,790, these are significantly lower than the eye-watering international fees international students have to pay — which are sometimes as high as £60,000 a year for the most prestigious courses.

But London has been resistant to the idea because its university sector says it depends on the cash to balance its books.

The Russell Group of research-intensive universities says the change would cost £580 million — money that administrators are skeptical the British Treasury would stump up to bridge the gap.

But a new idea now doing the rounds in Brussels is a halfway house, the two people — an EU diplomat and an EU official, both, like others in this story, granted anonymity to speak frankly — said.

While the EU is still seeking a cut in fees, its students would be expected to cover their costs to institutions. The result would be paying fees higher than domestic British students, but lower than other international students, from whom universities make a profit.

World.title: Merz’s fresh start quickly falls apart
World.content:
No one is yet saying out loud that Merz should go. But if his party performs poorly in three state elections in September, the crisis will likely become much harder to contain.

The drama has so far unfolded in two acts. The first began on July 14, when BILD — which, like POLITICO, is owned by Axel Springer — reported that Jens Spahn, the conservatives’ parliamentary group leader, and his husband had become parents through a surrogate mother in the United States.

“This feeling can hardly be put into words,” the paper quoted him as saying. The complication was plain enough: Surrogacy is banned in Germany, and the CDU has long opposed it, as had Spahn.

Patrick Schnieder arrives to attend the weekly Cabinet meeting in Berlin on June 24, 2026. | Ralf Hirschberger/ AFP via Getty Images

Merz’s standing has deteriorated since he took office in May 2025, with his support among voters falling as the far-right Alternative for Germany has surged to the top of the polls. The surrogacy controversy intensified the unease within the CDU.

The second act of the crisis was meant, in Merz’s telling, to be a liberation and a fresh start. Spahn, a long-standing rival whom Merz had always eyed warily, was made to resign, and a broader shake-up was supposed to quickly follow — only for things to fly off the rails.

On Thursday, Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder learned that he was to be dismissed and immediately told his staff by text message. But the man Merz had lined up to replace him was not yet convinced to take the job and withdrew.

World.title: Despite high inflation, Fed expected to hold rates steady for now
World.content:
The highly anticipated Federal Reserve policy meeting on Wednesday comes amid uncertainty over whether policymakers are losing patience with inflation and, if so, whether they are ready to turn their frustration into action. Expectations are tilting towards 'not yet'.

 

US economists largely expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged this time, but see the risk of a hike as significant, with many pricing in a rate rise for September.

The monetary policy decision comes as renewed tensions in the Middle East have sent oil prices soaring again, reigniting concerns that inflation could keep climbing in the world's biggest economy.

Besides the Iran war, other factors adding to inflationary pressure include President Donald Trump's tariffs on foreign goods and a surge of investment in data centres to power artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of computer chips, equipment and electricity.

A tamer-than-expected inflation report on June consumer prices seemed to offer officials breathing room to keep rates stable, with headline inflation coming in at 3.5% year-on-year, down from 4.2% in May, and core inflation at 2.6%, following a 2.9% reading in May. The decline was largely driven by changes in energy prices.

Inflation has been stuck above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told Congress earlier this month that he had "no tolerance'' for elevated inflation. Warsh is presiding over his second policy meeting this week.

Fed watchers Joseph Egelhof and Guneet Dhingra at BNP Paribas Securities say "policymakers' patience with high and persistent inflation is broadly exhausted, meaning there is a significant risk'' of a rate hike in September.

The federal funds target range has stood at between 3.50% and 3.75% since December 2025.

ING's regional head of research for the Americas, Padhraic Garvey, said: "The logic for no change centres, in part, on the calming in June inflation readings. President Trump has also helped pave an unchanged bias given the seeming renewed halt to hostilities with Iran. And from a macro perspective, the US economy is exhibiting vulnerabilities outside of tech."

Policymakers may also want to see more economic data. On Thursday, the Commerce Department will deliver the first look at economic growth between April and June and publish the Fed's preferred inflation measure – the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index – for June.

Overall, more than 30% of Wall Street traders predict that the Fed will raise rates this week, while 76% foresee a rate hike in September, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Several Fed policymakers have also argued that the Fed will have to raise rates to return inflation to the 2% target.

"Sternly staring at inflation until it melts before our withering gaze is not an option,'' Christopher Waller, an influential member of the Fed's governing board, said in a speech this month.

World.title: Rocking the Iron Curtain: How Queen’s 1986 Budapest concert cracked the Soviet Bloc
World.content:
The only stop on Queen's The Magic Tour inside the Eastern bloc was a historic milestone both politically and culturally. In mid‑1980s Hungary, hosting a Western stadium show of this scale demanded almost unimaginable logistical and political compromises.

 

Once the green light had arrived from the upper echelons of the ruling party, the gates of the Népstadion literally had to be rebuilt and the ground around them dug up so that the crew’s gigantic multi‑axle trucks could even get onto the pitch.

According to estimates and music‑industry insiders gossip, Queen received a fee of around €110,000 – roughly half of what they usually asked for a concert elsewhere. One reason was that Hungary at the time simply could not come up with the required amount in hard currency. The British rockers accepted the lower fee because in return they were allowed to shoot a concert film using virtually the entire then‑existing Hungarian film production capacity, and they secured the international distribution rights to the resulting film, Hungarian Rhapsody, which went on to generate huge profits worldwide.

We will rock you

The concert went far beyond a musical experience: it produced a collective social catharsis. The flawless lights and sound of a Western pop culture officially branded as decadent shocked and enthralled the Hungarian audience.

The British ambassador in Budapest Justin McKenzie Smith (r) and Denis O'Regan (l) standing beside Freddie Mercury's wax figure in the foyer of the residence Brit Nagykövetség

Young people who had previously encountered this world only on crackling reel‑to‑reel tapes while listening to Radio Free Europe or on smuggled vinyl suddenly felt as if they were at the very centre of the world. Queen showed a Budapest that was already tentatively opening up yet still living in confinement what professionalism and boundless creativity could do.

The fact that the British Embassy in Budapest marked the 40th anniversary with an exclusive event says a lot about the concert’s significance. Past and present met at the ambassador’s residence: while guests posed for photos with a strikingly lifelike was figure of lead singer Freddie Mercury on loan from Madame Tussauds Budapest (source in Hungarian), a tribute band in the background brought the era’s biggest hits back to life.

The diplomatic celebration was attended by photographer Denis O'Regan, who documented the tour’s key moments, and by Peter Freestone, Mercury’s former confidant and personal assistant.

Peter Freestone, Freddie's former assistant, at the Budapest event Brit Nagykövetség

Every heartbeat of the tour, from its tensions to its triumph in Budapest, was captured at close range by one man: Queen’s official photographer at the time, Denis O’Regan. At the anniversary event in Budapest, Euronews had the chance to speak to the legendary photographer, who offered a rare glimpse behind the Iron Curtain at a slice of rock history.

Freddie Mercury and Brian May rehearsing in Budapest – the never‑before‑seen Denis O'Regan photo was displayed at the ambassador's residence Brit Nagykövetség/Denis O'Regan

This commemoration was your initiative – so this 40th anniversary clearly means a lot to you as well. Do you feel this show was perhaps more special than the Western legs of the tour? Did it feel different from the other venues?

Denis O'Regan: It was very different; everyone knew it was going to be special. We came for six days, which was very unusual – on tour we usually only stay one or two days. Budapest became a legend in Queen’s story. But even as we were coming here, we already knew this was going to be something special. We travelled from Vienna by hydrofoil, on a boat called Gorbachev, and there were huge crowds waiting for us on the riverbank. The band’s manager, Jim Beach, said this was a very special time because Queen was the first rock band allowed to play in that stadium. He admitted they could have sold tickets for several nights, but the People’s Republic of Hungary didn’t want that because they were afraid the music might become a little too popular and subversive. So it remained one night – but that one night became a genuine cultural milestone for Hungary.

Denis O'Reid at the event Brit Nagykövetség

Would you say the Budapest concert in 1986 had a different atmosphere from the other stops on the tour?

Definitely. In London, for example, people go to see a lot of big bands and maybe start to take it for granted. But here there was something obviously very, very special. You could feel it that night. It was special for Queen too, because Freddie learned that Hungarian folk song. They put a huge amount of effort into the show – and into filming it. You could feel it in the streets as well; we were here for six days, so we experienced much more than just the concert.

Freddie Mercury during rehearsal before the Budapest concert Brit Nagykövetség/Denis O'Regan

I read in an interview that Queen asked to be kept away from the fans. Was that your experience? Because that’s not what we see in the film.

I never sensed that, not once. They were completely approachable – Brian even went off in a hot‑air balloon. I myself walked through the streets of Budapest several times with John Deacon. When we arrived on the hydrofoil, there were crowds waiting for us and nobody was held back. They completely surrounded Freddie’s car as well. I certainly never saw any attempt to keep fans away. I don’t know what happened at the hotel, or whether people even knew where Queen was staying, but from what I saw the mood everywhere was very open and relaxed.

From what you say, it sounds like you enjoyed your time here.

I felt happy, and I considered it an honour to be here. It’s funny, because even though they were global superstars, they too felt it was an honour to play here – because they were the first, and that was a big deal.

Would it be fair to say you eventually became friends with the stars? In another interview you said you had photographed so many rock legends that you almost became 'part of the furniture' for them.

I was always around them. Long before I even became a photographer, I knew I wanted to tour with David Bowie, Queen and the Rolling Stones. I had travelled around Europe by train, and that’s when I realised something: I wanted to spend my whole life travelling. I decided to combine those three things – music, photography and travel. Then I suggested they should take me with them on tour. In fact, it was all part of a conscious plan.

The lights of Budapest shining behind Freddie Mercury Brit Nagykövetség/Denis O'Regan

So in the end you were in the right place at the right time.

Yes – but I also made sure I was in the right place at the right time. And that I said the right thing at the right moment. I was the one who came up with the idea of taking a photographer along on tour. And it happened. I worked most extensively with David Bowie – I accompanied him on two world tours.

So you had the chance to get to know Freddie Mercury up close. How would you describe him?

He was very funny – that’s the first word that comes to mind. And he swore all the time. His language was terrible. He kept using the F‑word, which somehow made him even funnier. And what’s really interesting is that on and off stage he was essentially the same person. The biggest difference was probably that off stage he behaved a little more shyly – with people he didn’t know. But with those he let into his inner circle he could be incredibly blunt and cheeky. And he was the greatest showman who ever lived.

If you could choose just one photograph that best captures Freddie Mercury’s personality, which one would it be?

I wish I could show you two! I took two backstage shots of him: in one, Freddie is looking straight into the camera, already wearing his stage outfit. But a few minutes earlier I had taken a photo of him in his everyday clothes... (he demonstrates Freddie’s posture) ...completely relaxed. Once he put on his stage costume... (he mimics Freddie’s signature pose) he transformed in an instant.

Taking pictures is almost free today. It was nothing like that back then – it was very expensive. You had to buy all your film before you set off and then lug it around the world.

You actually saw the full transformation.

Exactly. I saw the same thing with Mick Jagger. I spent eight weeks on tour with the Rolling Stones. I was standing next to him backstage. Then he walked out onto the stage, and I moved round to the audience side... ...and suddenly he seemed ten years younger than the man I’d been talking to backstage just seconds before. I always thought: 'How does he do that?' His face changed. His energy too. The moment he stepped out in front of the crowd, everything inside him sprang to life.

Do you think photographing concerts or rock stars has changed a lot since you first started shooting bands?

Everything is much easier now. Taking pictures is almost free today. It was nothing like that back then – it was very expensive. You had to buy all your film before you set off and then lug it around the world. It was costly and limited. I always say it was like having a machine gun with a fixed number of bullets – once the film ran out, that was it. So you had to wait for the right moment. Today you can take thousands of images.

With a digital camera you can work in almost any light and you can fix almost anything. In our day there was no Photoshop. Now you can take excellent pictures even with a mobile phone – and you see the result instantly. In the past you sent off your film for processing and then waited a week or two to find out whether the pictures had even come out. It was a completely different world. But I love Photoshop and digital photography because you can use them anywhere.

Freddie signing the Embassy's guestbook Brit Nagykövetség/Denis O'Regan

So you’re clearly not against digital innovation.

Not at all. Young photographers often say to me: 'Things were so much easier for you.' And I always ask them: really? How was I supposed to know where a band was playing? There was no internet. How could I have got in touch with them? There were no mobile phones either. It was at least a hundred times harder. Many people say security is much tighter these days, and that’s true. Everything is more organised and more sophisticated now. But the opportunities are still there – just as they were. It’s simply that far more people are taking pictures, because photography has become cheaper and more accessible. When I started, hardly anyone wanted to do this. But I did.

I remember the first time I saw Led Zeppelin. Jimmy Page was playing his guitar with a violin bow. The rosin dust falling from the bow slowly drifted up into the beam of the spotlight while the sound echoed around the venue. And I thought: 'That moment has just gone forever. What a waste!' I wanted those moments to survive. I wanted to preserve them. That’s really where it all began. Later a friend told me I absolutely had to see David Bowie. So I went. It was during the Ziggy Stardust era. He came on stage in a silk kimono, with a girl on either side who, during the show, tore off parts of his costume. There was mime. There was theatre.

I remember thinking: 'I never knew a world like this existed.' Nobody else was doing anything like it. In that moment I knew I wanted to photograph him – not just because he was a fantastic performer, but because I wanted to hold on to those moments.

Finally, could you tell us a bit about your plans? I suppose you still work an awful lot.

Yes, although I don’t actually shoot that much anymore. These days I tend to work on different kinds of projects. For instance, there is a special sound studio in London with sixty speakers hidden in the walls and eight projection screens surrounding the visitor. Together we created an immersive experience called the David Bowie Experience. It brings together my photographs, my personal stories about David Bowie and his music. It turned into something really special. It’s even been selected for the programme of the Venice Film Festival, so I’ll be there in September. I’ve just finished a new David Bowie book as well. And there’s a new Queen book too. I brought a copy with me to Budapest – at the moment only four copies exist. A deluxe edition will follow later.

A new Queen exhibition will open in Montreux around Freddie Mercury’s birthday, which happens to coincide almost exactly with the Venice Film Festival. There is also a series of exhibitions planned in museums in Germany. That one will focus on David Bowie, as he would have turned eighty next January.

I’d like to make a documentary about the extraordinary people I’ve had the chance to work with over the years. I also want to turn these stories into a book and a podcast. I’ve already written most of the text. Now the goal is to shape the stories and the photographs that go with them into a single coherent whole. That’s the next big task.

The Tisza’s 'anthem' at the Népstadion: Spring Wind and the play of symbols

The undisputed high point of the 1986 Budapest concert – the moment that later became a generational myth – came when Freddie Mercury performed with only Brian May’s acoustic guitar for accompaniment. Reading the lyrics from his palm, he sang the Hungarian folk song "Tavaszi szél vizet áraszt" phonetically yet with stunning clarity. In the concert film, still regularly screened at the Uránia National Film Theatre and in art cinemas, you can clearly see the audience’s initial shock, which almost instantly gives way to a thunderous sing‑along from 78,000 voices.

In a peculiar twist of fate and Hungarian history, this classic folk song has recently acquired a completely new and powerful political and social context. Although the piece is originally about nature awakening, renewal and love, in Hungarian public life "Tavaszi szél" has become the unofficial anthem of the Tisza Party and of crowds calling for political change – a symbol of social discontent and new beginnings.

Of course, in 1986 Freddie Mercury could not possibly have foreseen the domestic political battles of 2020s Hungary; his choice was purely an act of paying respect to the host country. At the same time, the fact that the greatest rock singer in the world chose precisely this song and these metaphors, and had them sung by the crowd at a historic moment in Hungary’s long struggle for freedom, now feels almost prophetic, visionary in hindsight. As Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, who attended the anniversary celebration in Budapest, stressed in her speech, Freddie’s performance triggered a "cultural earthquake".

Hungarian Foreign minister Anita Orbán talking with Zsuzsa Körmendy and Csaba Lukács at the reception Brit Nagykövetség

The political legacy of "Hungarian Rhapsody"

The concert film Hungarian Rhapsody: Queen Live in Budapest (source in Hungarian), shot during the band’s Budapest appearance, is far more than a record of a hugely successful show. It is one of the 20th century’s most important Eastern European historical documents. The joint work of the British crew and the Mafilm studio professionally captured the moment when, for one night, music neutralised Cold War divisions and the rigid framework of dictatorship.

Queen’s visit offered tangible proof that, culturally and intellectually, Hungarian society wanted to belong to the West, even if the geopolitical reality at the time suggested otherwise. This realisation, and the collective sense of empowerment experienced in the Népstadion, gave Hungarians invaluable momentum in the run‑up to the regime change that followed barely three years later.

World.title: Parisian spot with five-step seasonal menu was just named the best new cocktail bar in the world
World.content:
The best new international cocktail bar has just been named at the Spirited Awards – and you can find it in Paris.

 

De Vie, which is located in the French capital’s Montorgueil quarter, was given the accolade at the 20th edition of the awards from Tales of the Cocktail Foundation (TOTCF).

The bar is known for its five-step seasonal tasting menu, served with snacks over the course of an hour and a half. Drinks are tasting portions, so the entire experience is the equivalent of three standard cocktails, and you can also opt for the non-alcoholic option.

As the menu is seasonal, drinks are constantly changing, but a sample on the website includes concoctions such as the strawberry, with oxidised strawberry, fig leaf wine and strawberry spirit; the fennel, with fennel spirit, fennel leaf cordial, and celery eau de vie; and the rhubarb, with cryo-concentrated rhubarb wine, rhubarb and crème fraîche liqueur.

You can also order à la carte drinks like the pepper, with charred pepper spirit, prickly pear eau de vie and herb stem cordial, and plates such as yellowtail tartare or agnolotti.

Satan’s Whiskers in London’s Bethnal Green was named the best international cocktail bar. The awards are split into best international, best US, and best overall.

The best cocktail bar in the world

A venue in Singapore took home the top prize, with FURA named the world’s best bar.

Named after the Swedish word for pine, the bar is all about sustainability and makes use of ingredients that are either in abundance, invasive or prevalent.

The creatively-named refreshments include “beans, beans the musical fruit”, which has Empirical soka, tonka bean, butter bean koji and pea shoot, and “get the worm”, featuring Altos Plata tequila, chilli, mealworm, orange and lime.

The food menu is equally innovative, with a jellyfish ceviche using an invasive spotted coral jellyfish and a somma mafaldine pasta with charred Talula Hill Farm purple corn.

World.title: The people building AI are asking governments to 'decelerate' the industry after models broke loose
World.content:
More than 1,000 employees from leading AI companies signed a petition on Tuesday urging the US government to take steps to "deliberately pace" the development of artificial intelligence.

 

Among the signatories were the Anthropic CEO, the head of research at OpenAI, the strategic lead of Google's AI subsidiary DeepMind and the chief scientist at Meta AI.

The petition calls for "the US government [to] support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."

"The world's leading AI companies believe they could be close to automating AI research. It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate AI progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems," the petition reads.

The call comes in response to a recent security scare after frontier AI models carried an autonomous cyberattack, escaping the controlled "sandbox" environment where the test was supposed to be carried out and breaking into the servers of code-sharing platform Hugging Face.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who did not sign the petition, said in an interview on the "Invest Like the Best" podcast on Tuesday that artificial intelligence developers may need to voluntarily slow the pace of advancement to give society time to adapt.

"This is the first sort of security incident that I felt very viscerally," Altman said on the "Invest Like the Best" podcast on Tuesday, adding that he was "a little surprised" that not more people were having similar reactions.

It was not the first time an AI model had operated beyond the control of its developers, but the latest incident was widely viewed as particularly alarming.

Have we reached the AI singularity?

A few days earlier, in an interview on the Relentless podcast, Altman said we had reached a point at which artificial intelligence surpasses human intelligence and starts advancing faster than people can predict or control — known as the "singularity".

Altman reflected that the singularity used to be a distant, half-joking topic of lunchtime conversation among colleagues a decade ago, but that has now changed.

Later in the same appearance, Altman pushed back against AI leaders who have warned about the technology's dangers, without naming Anthropic directly, though its CEO Dario Amodei is known for such warnings.

He said he intends to actively counter what he called "terrifying" alternative visions of AI's future.

World.title: Wildfires: Europe on track for worst year on record as burned area reaches size of Luxembourg
World.content:
Spain is the EU country that's been worst hit by this year's wildfires, recording the highest share of burned land in Europe relative to its size in 2026.

 

That's more than 200,000 hectares, or around 0.4% of the country’s territory, according to the EU's Earth observation programme Copernicus.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez warned that difficult hours lay ahead, after more than 90,000 people were forced to evacuate areas around Madrid and Ávila.

Neighbouring Portugal is also facing a severe fire season, recording the EU's second-highest proportion of burned land, at 0.3%.

On Monday, every district in northern and central Portugal, along with the southern district of Faro in the Algarve, was placed under the highest fire risk alert.

Yet some non-EU countries, like Ukraine or Montenegro, reported even worse rates.

How much damage have the 2026 wildfires done?

France was another country hit hard, with around 260,000 people evacuated, and the southwestern department of Gironde suffering the worst damage.

Meanwhile, the EU as a whole could be bound for its worst wildfire season on record.

The bloc has already endured around 1,200 fires in 2026, which is more than double the annual average of 569, says the EU's Forest Fire Information System.

So far, more than 250,000 hectares have gone up in flames, according to figures from the European Commission. To put that into perspective, that’s roughly the size of Luxembourg.

With much of the summer still ahead, the total is on track to pass 2025's record of more than 270,000 hectares.

Forest rangers take a break before returning to work on the fire near Condemios de Arriba, Guadalajara province, Spain, Wednesday, July 22, 2026 AP/Manu Fernandez

How are the fires affecting the environment?

Copernicus estimates that the 2026 wildfires have already spread more than 8 tonnes of CO₂ across the EU.

An average citizen emits around 5.55 tonnes over a whole year.

As "below-average rainfall" is also expected for this week, the situation is likely to get even worse, with "the strongest deficit stretching from France through the Alps and into the Balkans".

"Above-average rainfall spans Scandinavia and northern Europe, with the strongest surplus over Scandinavia," Copernicus said.

World.title: The Slovak village questioning its UNESCO status
World.content:
The picturesque village of Vlkolinec in Slovakia has been on UNESCO's World Heritage List since 1993. Vlkolinec was recently in the headlines for wanting to be taken off the list. DW visited the village to find out why.

From the headlines in the world's media, the story seemed simple: A tiny Slovak village wanted UNESCO to remove it from the World Heritage List because of the pressures of overtourism.

But that's not quite what is happening in Vlkolinec, central Slovakia.

Interviews with residents, local officials and visitors suggest that the debate was less about UNESCO itself than about how to protect a living community from the pressures of tourism.

Accelerated transformation

"Those who come with humility, to admire the village and understand how people lived here, are always welcome," said 68-year-old Anton Sabucha. "They don't bother me. It's the rude ones."

Sitting beneath an awning outside his wooden house, Sabucha leafed through a history of the village, pointing to photographs of neighbors and relatives. His wife brought out a tray of fried dough pastries.

Vlkolinec in bygone days: Anton Sabucha says that the village's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated its transformation Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW

He remembered when around 200 people lived in Vlkolinec. Today, only 17 remain year-round.

UNESCO did not create Vlkolinec's tourism problem. The village was designated a Folk Architecture Heritage Reserve in 1977, during the Communist era.

But Sabucha argued that its inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated the transformation, bringing visitors who too often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses.

Diminishing privacy

"You come out into your yard, wanting to sit quietly and have a coffee with your friends. Then the first tourist comes and asks, 'How are you? What's it like living here?' Then another. Then another," he told DW.

Sabucha has erected a barrier at the entrance to his property bearing the notices "No Trespassing" and "No Photos." He said that despite this, some visitors still wander into private gardens, trampling flowers and treating the village as an attraction rather than a community.

Vlkolinec resident Anton Sabucha says that some tourists often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses they come to admire Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW

"Someone sees the 'No Photos' sign and still has to take a picture. They simply don't respect people's privacy."

Disappearance of traditional village life

But the biggest loss, he said, has been the gradual disappearance of traditional village life.

The surrounding meadows are no longer cut, the old agricultural terraces have become overgrown and many of the people whose lives have shaped the landscape are gone.

Tourism income, he argued, has done little to reverse that decline.

Residents receive around €400 ($455) a year from ticket revenues — "barely enough to buy a pallet of briquettes for the winter" — while many of those who now earn a living from tourism no longer live in the village, he said.

"For an ordinary tourist, these are just wooden houses. For us, they're people. We know exactly who lived in each house."

A living village

Justine, a tourist visiting from France, said the village's appeal lay precisely in the fact that people still lived there.

"Usually places like this are museums. Here, people still live here. That's unique," she told DW.

When told that some residents wanted Vlkolinec removed from the UNESCO list because of tourism, she said she understood their frustration.

Why a Slovak village would like to lose its UNESCO status To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Having people walking around your village every day could become unpleasant," she said. "But at the same time, tourism also supports the region. It's difficult to know what's best."

UNESCO status helps preservation

Not everyone agrees that UNESCO is the problem.

Miro Parobek, who oversees tourism for the town of Ruzomberok, which administers Vlkolinec as a municipal district, acknowledged that tourism had brought challenges. But he argued that the answer was better management, not removing the village from the World Heritage List.

"Our first priority is to preserve the traditional architecture," Parobek told DW. "But our goal is also for this to remain a living village. We want to support the people who live here."

He said the town had already responded to residents' concerns by replacing large festivals with smaller cultural events, while residents now met regularly with local officials through a dedicated working group.

Miro Pirobek, head of Culture and Tourism in the nearby town of Ruzomberok, says that the priority is to preserve the traditional architecture of the village and support the people who live there Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW

The municipality also helped homeowners apply for grants to restore historical buildings and even provided twice-weekly transport into nearby Ruzomberok for older residents.

Parobek said every entrance ticket carried the same message: "Vlkolinec is not an open-air museum. Please respect the privacy of the people who live here."

Balancing tourism, heritage and residents' wishes

He acknowledged that the balance between protecting residents and welcoming visitors was not always easy.

Much of Parobek's optimism rested on plans that had yet to materialize.

Ruzomberok was seeking Norwegian funding for a package of measures aimed at reducing pressure on the village, including a park-and-ride below the hillside settlement, improved footpaths and drainage, the restoration of traditional barns and terraces, and the conversion of the former village school into a community and cultural center.

The project would also create more opportunities for local residents to work as guides and custodians, he said.

Is removal from the list possible?

Anton Sabucha is in a minority. But even if he somehow gets his wish, having Vlkolinec struck off the World Heritage List is an almost impossible task.

It looks unlikely that Vlkolinec will become the first site to be removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List at the request of its residents Image: Rob Cameron/DW

UNESCO has removed sites only three times since the program was established in 1978: Germany's Dresden Elbe Valley after the construction of a four-lane bridge, Liverpool's historical waterfront following large-scale redevelopment and Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary after most of the protected reserve was stripped of its status.

In each case, UNESCO acted because the sites had irreversibly lost the qualities for which they had originally been inscribed.

There is no precedent for a community asking to be removed voluntarily.

And there is no sign that Vlkolinec is about to become the first to succeed in its request.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with aiding terrorism
World.content:
Moscow has escalated its pressure on Telegram, accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.

Russia's Federal Security Service on Wednesday said it had charged Pavel Durov, the billionaire founder of the Telegram messaging app, with aiding terrorist activities.

The agency also issued an international warrant for his arrest.

The FSB said the charge formed part of "an ongoing criminal investigation" against Durov.

Why is Russia charging Durov?

The security service accused Telegram's management of failing to remove channels, chats and bots allegedly used to organize attacks and acts of sabotage inside Russia.

According to the FSB, Ukrainian intelligence services had used the platform to prepare and coordinate sabotage, terrorist attacks, mass killings and cyberfraud.

These actions, as well as crimes committed by what the FSB described as terrorist and extremist organizations, had allegedly caused numerous deaths, including those of women and children, as well as billions in material damage.

Soon after the news of the warrant broke, Telegram's account on X posted a picture of Durov giving a middle finger to the camera.

What does Russia say about Telegram?

Russia began restricting Telegram's operations in the country last August.

In February, communications regulator Roskomnadzor said Telegram was still failing to comply with Russian law and that restrictions would remain in place until the company met its requirements.

Putin's strategy behind Russia's largest missile attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russian courts have fined Telegram more than 100 million rubles (around $1,26 million, €1,1 million) since the beginning of this year, law enforcement sources told the Interfax news agency.

The penalties were imposed mainly for failing to remove content banned in Russia.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Monday said that officials had discussed restoring Telegram's full operations, but claimed the company's representatives had shown little initiative.

Who is Pavel Durov?

The Russian-born billionaire Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013. The platform currently boasts over a billion users.

Durov previously founded VKontakte, Russia's leading social network.

The tech mogul left Russia in 2014 after resisting demands to hand over user data, and is currently based in Dubai.

He describes himself as a libertarian and has repeatedly clashed with governments seeking greater access to the platform.

Durov has promoted Telegram as a defender of privacy and free speech, while critics say weak moderation has allowed propaganda, disinformation and criminal activity to flourish.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Germany: How weather extremes impact local agriculture
World.content:
Heat, drought, heavy rain and late frosts are taking a toll on German farmers. They increasingly respond with adapted varieties, new crops, modern breeding techniques and modified farming methods.

For many German farmers, the heat wave in late June couldn't have come at a worse time. While barley was already ready for harvest across much of Germany, the drought struck other crops during a particularly vulnerable stage of development.

"This year is another difficult one for farms," Horst Gömann of Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia Chamber of Agriculture told DW.

Corn has been particularly hard hit, as the extreme heat coincided with the flowering period, he said. "We're already seeing some corn plants failing to form cobs. That, of course, essentially amounts to a total crop failure," Gömann said.

In corn, the energy is concentrated in the cobs. If they're missing, yields plummet dramatically.

The heat wave in June, with peak temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius, hit other European growing regions even harder. According to a recent analysis by Coceral, the European association of grain traders, this reduced the value of the grain harvest in Europe by more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion), with France and Hungary suffering the greatest losses.

Due to the heat wave, Coceral lowered its expectations for grain production in the European Union and the United Kingdom by just under 9 million metric tons, a decline of 3%. The London-based research institute Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) even expects a 5% decline. Corn accounts for the largest share of the downward revision in Europe's grain forecast, representing about half of the adjustment.

A heat wave in late June impacted this year's harvest in Germany negatively Image: Boris Roessler/dpa/picture alliance

German farmers need to diversify

The weather also took its toll on wheat and barley. In some cases, barley was harvested several weeks earlier than usual.

According to Gömann, this year's barley harvest is likely to be slightly below average. For wheat, he expects losses of about 10%.

Risk diversification is therefore an important adaptation strategy. Instead of growing just one kind of grain, many farms are relying on different kinds with varying maturity rates.

"You never know when such extreme heat will strike," Gömann said. He explained that farmers who grow multiple varieties spread the risk across different stages of development.

Barley has a natural advantage in this regard. It matures earlier than wheat and often completes grain formation before the major early-summer drought sets in.

Experts say that irrigating is only worthwile with crops but not with all fruits Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

Fruit farming struggles with late frost and sunburn

While drought threatens crops in the fields, late frost is a major concern in fruit farming. Due to climate change and mild winter temperatures, flower buds, from which the fruit will eventually develop, form earlier. However, frosty nights can occur well into spring.

Many fruit growers, therefore, protect their blossoms with frost-protection sprinklers. Water is sprayed over the blossoms, forming a layer of ice. "This traps enough heat inside so that temperatures don't drop as low as they would without frost-protection sprinklers," explains Gömann. These systems can also be used for irrigation during long dry spells in summer.

There are also technical solutions for combating heat. Today, hail protection nets serve more than just protection against severe weather, as they also shade the fruit and prevent sunburn.

In addition, experiments are already underway in fruit and wine growing with semi-transparent photovoltaic films. They generate electricity and protect the plants from excessive sunlight while allowing enough light to pass through.

However, while irrigation is an important tool, Gömann believes it is not always economically viable. He said vegetables, potatoes and fruit generate high returns and justify the investment. He added that for grains or corn, irrigation is not worthwhile. "The costs are simply too high," he said.

The water comes primarily from groundwater. Despite frequent periods of drought, Germany is not a water-scarce country. "We basically still have enough water in Germany," the Gömann emphasized. The problem, he said, is rather the uneven distribution. Heavy rainfall occurs in winter, while dry spells are becoming more frequent in summer.

Scientists are experimenting with crop varieties that are more resilient to heat and drought Image: picture-alliance/dpa/F. Rumpenhorst

New breeds suitable for a warmer climate

Plant breeding plays a central role. Varieties whose genetic origins lie in warmer regions of Europe are already being cultivated in North Rhine-Westphalia.

"With wheat, for example, we're already making extensive use of genetics from France," said Gömann. The climatic conditions there have, in some respects, already shifted to Germany.

Grains with shorter stalks, known as semi-dwarfs, have been around for many years. Short stalks can bear significantly heavier ears, are less likely to snap during heavy rain, hail, or wind and require less water.

In addition, research is being conducted on wheat varieties with deeper roots. Current research at the German Julius Kühn Institute, the Federal Research Centre for Cultivated Plants, aims to develop wheat whose roots respond dynamically to drought by growing deeper only when water becomes scarce in the topsoil.

Farmers protect peach buds with a thin layer of ice from frosty temperatures in spring nights Image: Sebastian Willnow/dpa/picture alliance

Soybeans and millet are only niche products

The agricultural sector is also experimenting with new crops. Soybeans are now being grown in parts of Germany, albeit on a very small scale. Experiments are even being conducted with millet, a crop known from arid regions around the world, also only on a very small scale. Even winegrowing is slowly expanding further north, which is a visible sign of the shifting vegetation zones.

For Gömann, the condition of the soil is at least as important as new crop varieties. He said it is crucial to avoid soil compaction so that roots can penetrate deep into the ground.

Farmers, modern agriculture adapting to climate change

Farmers have always had to adapt to changing conditions, said Gömann. What's new, however, is the pace. While climate change used to take place over generations, now it is noticeable within just a few decades.

"The whole thing is happening quite quickly now," he said.

At the same time, modern agriculture has significantly better options than previous generations. New varieties are developed within a few years, and international breeding companies are continuously working on plants that are more tolerant of drought and heat.

For the agricultural expert, one thing is certain: the increase in extreme weather conditions in the past years is no coincidence. He sees the severe droughts of 2018 and 2019, as well as the recent heat waves, as part of a trend.

"This can certainly be attributed to the emerging climate change," Gömann told DW.

Agriculture must therefore continue to adapt, just as it has done for centuries, he noted, adding that it must do so much faster than before.

World.title: US: Trump's intelligence chief pick Jay Clayton confirmed by Senate
World.content:
Clayton's appointment comes as Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the midterms.

The US Senate on Tuesday confirmed Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence at a time when President Donald Trump has started reiterating his false claims about the 2020 election, which he lost.

The 51-47 vote in the Senate was along party lines with Republicans supporting the appointment and Democrats voting against.

After the vote, Trump heaped praise on Clayton posting on Truth Social: "Jay is outstanding in every way, and will do a spectacular job as Director!"

Clayton stresses he isn't 'an election denier'

Clayton will now lead the 18 intelligence agencies, including the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), National Security Agency (NSA), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which have been reeling from leadership turmoil and staff cuts.

He is a former Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) chairman and US attorney for the Southern District of New York.

Democrats opposed Clayton's nomination after he repeatedly declined during his confirmation hearing to explicitly state that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election, saying only that the result had been "certified."

"I'm not an election denier," Clayton said, without directly answering the question.

Trump renews voter fraud claims

Clayton replaces Tulsi Gabbard, who resigned in June, and Trump temporarily installed Bill Pulte as acting intelligence chief.

Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no national security experience, oversaw a tumultuous tenure marked by a roughly 30% staff reduction and the release of 2020 intelligence documents detailing China's capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system.

Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the US midterm elections.

California Democratic Senator Adam Schiff told CNN that Clayton's refusal to unequivocally state that Biden won the 2020 election "suggests that if the president [Trump] wants the intelligence agencies to cook up something to justify voter interference in the midterm elections, that Jay Clayton doesn't have the backbone to stand up to him."

07/29/2026 July 29, 2026 Venezuela protests after Araghchi's remarks

Venezuela has summoned Iran's ambassador in Caracas to protest what it described as "disparaging and inappropriate" remarks about the country's institutions and authorities.

The Foreign Ministry said Ambassador Ali Chegini was handed a formal note of protest on Tuesday. While Venezuelan diplomats did not specify what prompted the move, the complaint appears to relate to recent remarks by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi about negotiations with the United States.

"This is not Venezuela, where they take one person and everyone else gets scared and backs down," Araghchi said, apparently referring to the US capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and the subsequent shift in relations between Caracas and Washington.

Venezuela demanded "an end to any reference or comparison that undermines the dignity, sovereignty, institutions or reputation of Venezuela," the ministry said on Telegram.

Venezuelans want elections — but when will they get them? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Relations between Tehran and Caracas have been particularly close since the presidency of the late Hugo Chavez, with both governments united by their opposition to the United States.

Iran was one of the main allies of Nicolas Maduro's government, particularly during Venezuela's fuel shortages in 2020, when Caracas turned to Tehran for petrol.

Maduro is now being held in New York after his capture in Caracas on January 3. Under acting President Delcy Rodriguez, Venezuela and the US have restored diplomatic ties and continued to move closer in recent months.

World.title: Japan: Rescue 'race against time' after deadly earthquake hits Kumamoto
World.content:
Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, at least two women were killed after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon, triggering emergency warnings and prompting authorities to assess the extent of the damage.

On Wednesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said 13 people have been found dead since the earthquake struck. She added that many other people were still missing, suggesting the death toll was not final.

What do we know about the rescue efforts?

By Wednesday, over 9,000 people were in evacuation centers amid the rescue efforts.

"We have received reports of seven people with serious injuries and 29 with minor injuries. Furthermore, as of 7:00 am today (2200 GMT Tuesday), 9,186 people have sought refuge in 506 evacuation centers across five prefectures, including Kumamoto and Fukuoka," government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.

At least two of the victims died in a shopping mall in Kashima and the third died in a building collapse in a town near the epicenter.

Japan's public broadcaster, NHK, reported that "many people" were trapped inside the shopping mall damaged by the earthquake.

Several people were rescued from the mall, including a person who was reported to be in cardiopulmonary arrest.

The collapse of the mall followed an explosion likely triggered by a gas leak, NHK reported.

"Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible," Takaichi told reporters ‌at her office in ⁠Tokyo ⁠a day after the quake struck.

Authorities assess damage as tsunami threat eases

Prime Minister Takaichi also said initial reports indicated multiple injuries, damage to civilian infrastructure, and fires in several affected areas.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said.

"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed," she added.

Although the earthquake caused widespread disruption and temporarily raised fears of a tsunami, officials later confirmed that the threat had subsided and that Japan's coastline was no longer in danger.

"This earthquake occurred inland, and no tsunami activity has been observed so far," a spokesperson for the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said. "For this reason, we hope to lift the tsunami advisory at a relatively early stage, depending on future sea level conditions."

The earthquake struck at 4:27 p.m. local time and registered the highest possible level of seven on Japan's Shindo intensity scale, which measures ground shaking Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

Power and nuclear facilities remain safe

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported that no abnormalities were detected at three nearby nuclear power plants, providing reassurance in a country still sensitive to nuclear safety concerns following the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

However, the earthquake disrupted electricity supplies across the region. According to Kyushu Electric Power, approximately 45,000 households and facilities in Kumamoto temporarily lost power following the tremor.

Several major industrial facilities are located near the earthquake zone, including operations belonging to Sony and the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker. Sony stated that it was evaluating conditions at its facilities, while TSMC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Japan's long history of major earthquakes

Kumamoto is no stranger to devastating seismic events.

In 2016, the region was struck by two major earthquakes, first a magnitude 6.5 quake and then a magnitude 7.3 tremor two days later. The disaster claimed 273 lives, injured more than 2,800 people. Thousands of buildings were either damaged or destroyed, making it one of Japan's most destructive recent earthquake disasters.

More recently, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck northern Japan on June 25, causing little damage and no fatalities. Earlier this year, on April 20, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in northern Japan injured at least ten people and shook high-rise buildings as far away as Tokyo, prompting authorities to issue a temporary advisory warning of an increased risk of even stronger earthquakes. That advisory was lifted a week later.

Powerful earthquake hits southern Japan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the world's most earthquake-prone nations

Japan sits along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the most active seismic zones on Earth where four major tectonic plates meet.

Home to approximately 125 million people, the country experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year and accounts for roughly 18% of the world's seismic activity.

While most tremors are relatively minor, Japan remains haunted by memories of the catastrophic magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami that struck the country's northeast coast in March 2011. The disaster killed or left missing around 18,500 people and triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis.

Tuesday's earthquake demonstrated the country's preparedness systems, emergency response capabilities, and monitoring of critical infrastructure.

As authorities continue to assess the impact of the Kumamoto quake, residents are being urged to stay alert for potential aftershocks and follow official safety guidance.

World.title: Zelenskyy visits Trump as Ukraine seeks stronger air defense
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is seeking stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the United States for talks with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, saying Kyiv's top priority was securing stronger air defense and strategic cooperation as Russia intensified attacks.

Trump welcomed Zelenskyy to the White House late on Tuesday morning local time, ahead of the funeral for Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who passed away earlier this month.

Images taken from behind the fences at the White House showed Zelenskyy exiting a car ready to enter the building.

White House press ‌secretary Karoline Leavitt described the meeting, which was behind closed doors, as "positive and productive."

Zelenskyy thanked Trump for the "good meeting," hailing the Republican administration's support to Kyiv in its war against Russia.

“The President and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help,” said Zelenskyy on X. “We also spoke about diplomacy — it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated.”

Later, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that the meeting "went very well!"

Zelenskyy was spotted arriving at the White House soon after his arrival in the US on Tuesday Image: Jemal Countess/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

"Our number-one priority is anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation with America. Peace needs to be brought closer," Zelenskyy had said in a post on X after arriving in the US.

US-Ukraine deal on Patriot production recently announced

The long-strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have shown modest signs of improvement in recent weeks.

Since returning to office in January last year, Trump largely stopped direct US arms shipments to Ukraine, instead leavingEuropean allies to buy American weapons and supply them to Kyiv.

However, Washington remains a key ally, providing intelligence and access to the Starlink satellite network used by Ukrainian frontline troops to communicate.

In a sign of improving ties, Trump, in a meeting with Zelenskyy in Turkey earlier this month, pledged to help Ukraine produce Patriot air defense systems, and said Kyiv would be able to produce them "pretty quickly."

This has been a long-running request from Kyiv in order to counter Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes

More than four years have passed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war brokered by the Trump administration, both sides have stepped up long-range strikes.

Russia said on Tuesday that more than 390 Ukrainian drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, damaging residential buildings.

Russian state media also reported that Russian forces struck two vessels, including a ship in the Black Sea that Moscow claimed was transporting military supplies for Ukraine, according to Reuters.
