“We need to create conditions where women no longer have to choose one or the other. They should be able to have both. It is important that women can pursue formal employment while also having time for their families. Otherwise, the country will face demographic challenges,” she said.

When Sargsyan talks about creating better conditions for working women, she refers in particular to expanding access to nurseries and kindergartens, as well as developing childcare centres for young children.

Remote work is already available in Armenia, and working mothers can take advantage of it with their employer’s consent. The government has also recently introduced a “parental hour” policy. Under the new rules, working parents with children under the age of 12 can either arrive at work later or leave earlier. Parents with one or two children can reduce their working day by 30 minutes. Those with three or more children can shorten it by one hour. However, experts say these measures do not go far enough to create a truly family-friendly working environment.

Lusine Sargsyan stresses that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on household responsibilities means some women effectively work two full-time jobs. In addition to unpaid domestic work, they spend another 40 hours a week working for an employer.

She argues that this is problematic both economically and from a human rights perspective because women are left with little or no time for themselves. She also says excessive workloads reduce productivity at work and affect the quality of care they can provide for their children at home.

Sargsyan emphasises that workplaces need to become more family-friendly. That would allow women to fulfil their potential while also spending meaningful time with their families.

“Employers need to recognise that their employees have families. It is extremely important that women do not live with a constant sense of guilt. They should not feel guilty about spending too little time with their families. Nor should they worry at home about work they did not finish,” she explained.

Both Sargsyan and Jrbashyan stressed that many women are highly productive and, in many cases, better educated than men.

They argue that the country needs to create better conditions for women to work. Otherwise, the economy risks missing out on the higher value they could generate.

At the same time, both experts stressed that they are not arguing every woman should have formal employment or receive pay for household work. Instead, they say women should have the freedom to decide how they want to organise their lives. They believe giving women that choice would benefit the country’s economy, improve business performance and create a healthier family environment.

Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

World.title: GYLA: ‘Georgia has effectively created an informal ‘morality police’, which could become a new form of violence’
World.content:
GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) has responded to reports about the creation of a movement to protect traditional values, warning that alongside existing legal restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and civic participation, the initiative could introduce new mechanisms of violence in the country.

The movement was announced on 26 July by MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili and several supporters. At a press briefing, he said the organisation would “respond immediately” to issues involving the country’s ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. Kartvelishvili said the movement would be “highly active, respectable and constructive”, adding that any “patriotic Georgian” would be welcome to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

GYLA described the initiative as the creation of an informal “morality police”, warning that it poses a threat to freedom of expression in Georgia.

According to the organisation, “everything suggests that the group’s aim may be to informally monitor, intimidate or pressure people who are critical of the authorities.”

GYLA’s lawyers added that “attempts to establish vigilante groups in the country are particularly alarming” given the rise in violence and intimidation targeting government critics in recent years.

GYLA said members of the new group are using defamatory and disinformation-laden language that closely mirrors narratives promoted by the authorities and pro-government media.

In particular, the group says it is launching a campaign “against people and organisations funded from abroad, enslaved to foreign interests and driven by a perverse ideology.”

According to GYLA, the group’s statements contain signs of incitement to violence. The lawyers pointed in particular to its declaration that “if circumstances leave no alternative, members of the group will not be afraid of going to prison.”

GYLA said the group has already demanded an apology from stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, who was recently severely beaten in the street after making a joke referring to Georgian literary classic Nodar Dumbadze.

The group has also asked prosecutors not to seek a prison sentence for the person accused of attacking Okriashvili. Otherwise, its representatives warned, there could be reprisals, according to GYLA.

“We will hold people accountable for every action and comment that insults the dignity of the Georgian people,” the group said in a statement cited by GYLA.

GYLA said such statements echo remarks made by senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party which, in the organisation’s view, call for greater control over freedom of expression.

The organisation also noted that attacks by third parties targeting people critical of the government were widely documented during the 2024 protests and in the months that followed.

According to GYLA, such incidents were often accompanied by statements from state officials appearing to support the attackers or by an inadequate response from law enforcement.

“Against this background, it is clear that the creation of a vigilante group and its declared intention to police citizens’ freedom of expression are closely linked to the state’s ongoing normalisation of violence,” GYLA said.

The organisation noted that Georgian criminal law prohibits the creation, leadership or membership of illegal armed or violent groups. It also bans the establishment of associations, or participation in them, if their activities involve violence against individuals.

GYLA said law enforcement authorities must take all measures provided for by law to prevent violence or intimidation against people exercising their fundamental rights.

According to the organisation, “pro-government media are actively contributing to the demonisation and targeting of individuals, which may amount to incitement to violence and complicity in it. The inaction or delayed response of state institutions creates an environment that enables violence to spread.”

GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

World.title: Georgian banks to continue servicing local subsidiaries of sanctioned Russian energy giant Inter RAO
World.content:
Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

The National Bank of Georgia has announced that the country’s commercial banks will continue providing services in the national currency to Telasi, despite the company being owned by Russian energy giant Inter RAO, which was included in the European Union’s latest, 21st package of sanctions against Russia. The central bank confirmed the decision to BM.GE.

At the end of July, the European Union imposed sanctions on the Russian state-controlled energy company Inter RAO. Through its subsidiaries, the company is the indirect owner of Georgia’s electricity distribution companies Telasi and Telmiko, as well as the Khramhesi-1 and Khramhesi-2 hydropower plants.

The National Bank said that Telasi itself is not included on any sanctions list and that its uninterrupted operation is essential for the country’s population and economy. According to the central bank, while compliance with international sanctions is important, it is equally crucial to ensure the uninterrupted provision of essential services to the public.

The National Bank said that each sanctions-related case would be assessed on its individual merits. As a result, banks will continue providing services to Telasi “in compliance with the applicable sanctions regime, as well as in accordance with their own internal policies and risk assessment procedures.”

Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

World.title: Man who allegedly filmed two decades of sexual abuse to stand trial
World.content:
A southern NSW man is set to stand trial accused of filming himself raping and assaulting a woman over two decades.

The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, is facing allegations he sexually assaulted the woman at various properties in the Snowy Mountains and the Riverina between 2007 and 2025.

The man, aged in his 60s, appeared before Sydney's Downing Centre District Court via audio-visual link on Wednesday, where he pleaded not guilty to 45 charges.

It took about 20 minutes for the court to read out each charge one-by-one, which included 32 counts of sexual intercourse without consent.

It is alleged most of the assaults took place between 2007 and 2024 at Adaminaby, as well as parts of the Riverina, including Gundagai.

The man pleaded not guilty to all charges on Wednesday. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

Crown prosecutors allege the man made hours of recordings of the alleged abuse over 15 years, which the court heard would form part of their case in an upcoming criminal trial.

The man also pleaded not guilty to other charges including aggravated sexual assault while inflicting bodily harm, assault causing bodily harm, and acting with intent to influence a witness.

Concerns for jury

The court heard during Wednesday's arraignment hearing that the complainant in the matter had recently died, but the prosecution would still go ahead with the trial.

"All of the evidence is on video," crown prosecutor Katrina Mackenzie told the court.

Crown prosecutors said they would also rely on recorded statements from police interviews with the complainant.

Ms Mackenzie told the court that 12 hours of footage depicting the alleged assaults would be shown at the trial, but she had "mental health concerns" about a jury watching the recordings.

"If a jury was observing it [the recordings], we would need to take a lot of breaks," Ms Mackenzie told the court.

Defence lawyer Roland Keller agreed he too would "be asking for the jury to have a break" after watching relevant parts of the footage, which was recorded over 15 years.

Both parties agreed a judge-alone trial would be more suitable.

The legal teams are expected to formally apply for such at a hearing in August.

Justice Christoper O'Brien scheduled the two-week trial in the Queanbeyan District Court for April 2027.

The court heard that less than a dozen witnesses were expected to give evidence at next year's trial, including community members and police.

The accused man was also granted conditional bail on Wednesday, to stay at a property in the Riverina until the trial next year.

World.title: Cult inquiry recommends outlawing coercive control in groups
World.content:
Survivors of cults and high-control groups have welcomed a landmark report that recommends outlawing coercive control in group settings.

A parliamentary investigation has recommended the world-leading laws be enacted in Victoria within three years.

For survivors of high-control groups, often referred to as cults throughout the inquiry, the "monumental" report offers a sense their experiences were heard, and there was hope ahead.

Ryan Carey is a former member of the Geelong Revival Centre and co-founded Stop Religious Coercion Australia.

"We were told that this would never happen and no government would take us seriously because there's religion involved," Mr Carey said.

" This legislation will save lives, I have no doubt about that. "

Ryan and Catherine Carey both left the Geelong Revival Centre. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

The lower house's Legal and Social Issues Committee wants the Victorian Law Reform Commission to review legislative options within two years, before group-based coercion is criminalised by 2029.

Through months of public hearings, the inquiry into the recruitment methods and impacts of cults and organised fringe groups heard allegations of child and sexual abuse in dozens of groups.

The committee heard harrowing stories from people who said they had grown up in groups where leaders controlled most of their daily lives.

Key recommendations: Introduce legislation to criminalise group‑based coercion by February 2029, based on options listed in a future report from the Victorian Law Reform Commission.

Establish a formal lived experience advisory body to co-design policy and reforms.

Strengthen laws to better protect children, establishing reforms to improve child protection where children are raised or recruited into high-control groups.

Improve training for frontline professionals. Provide police, teachers, health workers, child protection staff and family violence workers with specialised training about coercive high-control groups

Develop public education campaigns explaining recruitment techniques, coercive control and warning signs.

Improve access to trauma-informed counselling, housing assistance, legal support and employment assistance for those leaving groups.

The resulting report includes 39 recommendations and deliberately adopts a behaviour-based approach, focusing on coercive and controlling conduct rather than religious or ideological beliefs.

It recommends training for people working with children, a public awareness campaign and better support for people who have left high-control situations.

Frontline training

For Laura McConnell, who grew up in the secretive Truth Two By Twos, a safe person would have been "life changing".

But there was no-one to flag the conditions she was living in and no-one to show her that the rules she lived by could be challenged.

"I'm hoping that over time, if safe people can help children get out of these situations, that we minimise the number of people, children still in there, but then also we give them pathways out," Ms McConnell said.

Ms McConnell said she was 19 when she was shunned after pushing back on the life expected of her in the highly religious group and was left to start a new life, without any support.

Laura McConnell shared her experiences about leaving Truth Two By Twos with the inquiry. (Supplied: Laura McConnell)

Ms McConnell said the cult she was in was religious, and that the inquiry was about identifying behaviour, and in no way was limited to religion.

"This is about group-based coercive control; this is not about belief, it's not even about cults," Ms McConnell said.

"It's about a set of behaviours and understanding how to both stop those behaviours and support people who want to leave them.

"Many, many people are not choosing to join a high-control group; they are born in there, and then they have limited options to leave safely."

Ms McConnell's submission was among 317 made to the parliamentary committee.

Clare-Heath McIvor says no victim should have to prove their group is a cult. (Supplied: Clare Heath-McIvor)

In its report, the committee made an explicit choice not to give a definition of the word "cult".

Clare Heath-McIvor is the head of the Survivors of Coercive Cults and High-Control Groups and welcomed the "vitally important" move.

"No victim should have to prove their group is a cult before proving that group-based coercive control and abuse occurred, or that it mattered," she said.

"Any group can be a cult — multi-level marketing cults, yoga cults, political cults and more all exist.

"Cults are not a phenomenon of belief, but coercive control and domination across multiple domains of life."

Homeschooling review

One recommendation specifically implores the Victorian government to increase and diversify young people's contact with multiple reporting channels, particularly for those who are isolated.

It also involves reviewing home schooling arrangements in Victoria to ensure greater contact and connections with government schools.

Ms Heath-McIvor was home-schooled from grade one to year 12 and said it created huge challenges as she became an adult.

"There are legitimate reasons to homeschool, but one reason we often see is so that they can limit contact between the children and the outside world," she said.

"If there's an abusive situation, who does the child raise that with?

"Educational neglect can completely go unchecked in home-schooled communities; there aren't enough checks or safeguards to make sure children are safe, educated and properly cared for."

Annabelle Cleeland was the inquiry committee's deputy chair. (Supplied: Annabelle Cleeland )

In its report, the committee acknowledges that oversight of parental decisions would raise legitimate questions about religious freedom, but the current balance leaves a cohort of children without adequate protection.

Annabelle Cleeland is a National Party MP and led the committee as deputy chair.

"You don't want to over-legislate and remove people's freedom of faith or belief, but at the same time we need to make sure those that are most vulnerable in our community are protected as well," Ms Cleeland said.

"It's a fine line; it was something we really grappled with."

While a homeschooling review and potential solutions were not thoroughly outlined in the report, a proposed example was ensuring home-schooled children attend some activities onsite at government schools.

Ms Cleeland told the ABC she genuinely believes implementing the recommendations will protect people in future.

"Most people who were caught up in these high coercive control groups, they never felt like there was a point of recruitment, but eventually they lost their financial independence, their mental health, their physical independence, their extraordinary pressure and time that they had to be involved in these groups as well," Ms Cleeland said.

"Listening to what coercive control and cult involvement does to a person and their children and the years that follow and that disruption and how much they carry that trauma."

The Victorian government has six months to respond to the recommendations in the committee's final report.

World.title: Investors gave Capital Guard $17 million for a bond scheme that didn't exist
World.content:
Tammy Lindrum is trying to make sense of the encounters that took place before her $750,000 nest egg vanished and her prominent family's legacy was scarred.

There was a face-to-face meeting at an office in Melbourne's bustling Collins Street business precinct in September.

In January, a fun evening of champagne and cigars alongside a business executive "with a very big personality", at an upmarket bar.

And then, the generous $50,000 offer to help Ms Lindrum honour her prominent family's legacy.

Tammy Lindrum's late great-uncle and godfather, Walter Lindrum, is widely regarded as one of the greatest billiards players in history. (ABC News)

Ms Lindrum told 7.30 the experience she had with wealth management firm Capital Guard "still doesn't feel real".

But the company was real and operating with a valid Australian Financial Services Licence.

The executive Ms Lindrum and her husband John Wickham had been meeting in person was the company's head of finance, Vassos Dimitriou.

Ms Lindrum first invested with Capital Guard in September last year when she decided to buy corporate bonds.

Investors who buy bonds are essentially lending money to the governments and companies that issue them, in exchange for regular interest payments.

She was initially pleased with her investment and received regular interest payments on her account.

Her husband was considering investing too.

When the couple met Mr Dimitriou for drinks in January he told Ms Lindrum if she bought more bonds, Capital Guard would become a major sponsor for the network she set up to support women in cue sports.

Capital Guard investor Tammy Lindrum fears her $750,000 nest egg is gone and her family's sporting legacy has been damaged. (ABC News: Nico White)

She had launched the group in memory of her late father, world snooker champion Horace Lindrum, and her late great uncle, billiards legend Walter Lindrum.

"I was over the moon," she told 7.30.

As part of the $50,000 sponsorship deal, Capital Guard provided marketing material promoting its partnership with Ms Lindrum's Women's Billiards and Snooker Network.

Ms Lindrum was offered a $50,000 sponsorship deal by Capital Guard. (ABC News)

She now believes she was used for her recognisable family name.

Her relationship with Capital Guard rapidly unravelled in May, after she received a tip-off the company may not be what it seemed.

"[I felt] sick. Sick to the stomach," Ms Lindrum said.

" I'd done so much research and this is a company that is registered with ASIC. It has an ABN. It has a financial licence. "

Her worst fears were confirmed in the weeks that followed, when she asked Capital Guard's account managers to refund the capital she had invested.

She was met with a series of excuses, before, for the first time, she didn't receive her monthly interest payment.

In late June, ASIC cancelled Capital Guard's licence for dishonest conduct. It alleged the company was selling bonds that did not exist.

Ms Lindrum said she has been unable to reach Capital Guard ever since.

Capital Guard's licence was cancelled in June. (Supplied)

"Their emails, their website was pulled down. Everything is gone. You can't find them," she said.

Ms Lindrum is not just worried about her savings. She is concerned her involvement has tarnished the family legacy and the women's network she had worked hard to build.

"Setting up this network was my contribution to my family's legacy," Ms Lindrum said.

" This destroys me. Absolutely destroys me. "

Millions of dollars missing

This week, the NSW Supreme Court approved an application by ASIC to wind up Capital Guard after an investigation by the corporate watchdog allegedly found around 80 investors transferred $17.4 million to the company for bonds.

Most of that money cannot be found.

It is alleged $9 million was transferred to crypto platforms and another $4.1 million to currency exchanges.

Investors 7.30 spoke to were furious to learn Capital Guard had been on ASIC's radar for months before the company's licence was cancelled.

ASIC found Capital Guard had engaged in dishonest conduct, including falsifying documents and selling an investment product that didn’t exist. (Supplied)

In May last year, Macquarie Bank issued a public warning about scammers posing as representatives from Capital Guard, promoting fake bank-branded bonds.

In July, the bank formally complained about Capital Guard to ASIC.

7.30 understands others in the financial services industry also raised complaints with the regulator around the same time.

In September, ASIC launched a formal investigation into Capital Guard.

But the company kept trading for another 10 months until the end of June this year, when ASIC cancelled its Australian Financial Services Licence.

'Trail of victims'

Licensed private investigator Ken Gamble told 7.30 he named Mr Dimitriou from Capital Guard in an intelligence report to the Australian Federal Police in March.

The report contained information from a source, who made allegations about a group of foreign nationals overseas.

"[The foreign nationals] were in the process of setting up financial payment gateways in Australia," Mr Gamble said.

Mr Gamble was concerned because one of the foreign nationals identified is suspected of being a key player in a multi-million dollar scam he investigated in 2023.

Ken Gamble is a private investigator who works closely with the anti-scam unit run by the AFP. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

"Those perpetrators had left a trail of victims in Australia," Mr Gamble said.

The source also alleged Mr Dimitriou had been communicating with the group.

A lawyer for Mr Dimitriou did not respond to the allegations when contacted by 7.30.

Vassos Dimitriou was the previous director of Capital Guard. (ABC News)

The AFP declined to comment on what it had done with the information in Mr Gamble's report.

Corporate records show Mr Dimitriou was the previous director of Capital Guard.

He held the position for three months, before Melbourne man Mark Tasiyan took over as the sole director and shareholder in October 2024.

The court heard this week that Mr Tasiyan told ASIC he was not involved in the operation of Capital Guard — but he did open bank accounts for the company, before providing the log-in details to Mr Dimitriou.

The court also heard Mr Dimitriou provided falsified financial records for the company to an auditor.

A retirement in ruins

Perth man Ziggy Szmidt believes he would still have his retirement savings if action against the company sooner had been taken sooner.

In February this year, Mr Szmidt decided to invest the $700,000 he earned during his decades-long civil engineering career in corporate bonds through Capital Guard.

Ziggy Szmidt fears he has lost his retirement savings after investing $700,000 with Capital Guard. (ABC News: West Matteeussen )

"I did what should be done, because … I [ran] a few companies in my life and for me it was obvious to check the company," he said.

He checked the company's ASIC records, including its ABN, CAN and its financial services licence.

"The company was established in 2014, so it means they were on the market for maybe 12 years. So no suspicious things," he said.

He decided to diversify his portfolio by investing in seven different bonds, so his risk was reduced.

He started receiving returns on his investment until June this year, when his interest payment didn't appear in his account.

His Capital Guard account manager told him on the phone the issue would be fixed by the following business day.

But the money never arrived — and the company has been uncontactable.

Mr Szmidt said he feared his decision to invest with Capital Guard has destroyed the plans he and his wife had for their retirement.

Mr Szmidt has taken up extra shifts as a rideshare driver. (ABC News: West Matteeussen )

"We didn't expect some extra cars … or big houses," he said.

"[I just wanted] to live as I can. When you turn 70, there's not much you can do, but … now I did [a] hip replacement, and my wife did [a] knee operation, we can move a bit more than before."

They had wanted to spend more time with family overseas and help their adult children financially.

Instead, Mr Szmidt has been working more shifts as a rideshare driver.

He started the job to keep his mind active, but he now believes he will have to continue doing it to make ends meet.

"But next year, I am 72. So how long will I do it?" he said.

"When you are young, you can start from the beginning, do something different … but we are [a] retired old couple."

The Polish migrant said the incident had shaken his faith in his adopted country of 25 years.

He is shocked this could happen when he was dealing with "real people … with real licences … and real permissions [to operate]."

"I trusted Australia. That's why I migrated here. ASIC knew … and they did nothing," he said.

ASIC can't trace funds

Mr Gamble believes there needs to be much tougher rules around obtaining an Australian Financial Services Licence.

"I'm involved in other investigations that involve … foreign-based criminal syndicates purchasing Australian companies that have an Australian Financial Services Licence, so they can give themselves credibility and obviously convince investors they're legitimate," he said.

"There needs to be much stricter vetting."

The private investigator also believes ASIC's response to the allegations against Capital Guard was too slow.

"There needs to be a rapid response, and I don't believe there was a rapid response into this case," he said.

A spokesperson for ASIC told 7.30 in a statement: "This work is complex, and, in matters of this kind, we need to carefully investigate the operation of the entity before we decide what action to take in a way that does not precipitate investor losses."

This week, liquidators were appointed to take control of Capital Guard, investigate its affairs and attempt to recover any assets it may have.

It may however prove difficult.

"[ASIC] has not been able to trace where the funds have gone. In terms of cryptocurrency wallets and it has also not been able to identify other assets Capital Guard currently holds," ASIC's barrister Stephanie Patterson told court this week.

" It does not look good, Your Honour. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Breaking: Mother attended police station day before murder-suicide, police say
World.content:
The mother at the centre of the horrific murder-suicide in South Australia's South East attended a police station the day before she and her daughter were found dead, police have confirmed.

The bodies of Helena Wright, 36, and her 23-month-old daughter from Compton were spotted in the water on Monday, after her car was found abandoned with its engine running near Port MacDonnell.

Ms Wright's three-month-old son remains missing but police said the formal search was called off this afternoon after they received advice the child could not have survived.

In a statement, they confirmed Ms Wright had attended the local police station on Sunday, and that police conducted a welfare check the following morning.

"South Australia Police can confirm Helena Wright attended the Mount Gambier Police Station on Sunday 26 July where she spoke with police," police said in a statement.

"Police can also confirm as a result of a call from a friend received at about 0928 hours on Monday 27 July a patrol conducted a welfare check at the home address of Ms Wright.

"No-one was located at that time."

Police said they received reports from members of the public, at 11:13am on Monday, of Ms Wright's car at Cape Northumberland near Port MacDonnell.

"As this matter is now subject to a coronial investigation, SAPOL will provide all relevant information and evidence to the coroner," they said.

"It is not appropriate to comment further while coronial proceedings are underway."

World.title: Taiwan to stop buying PNG gas on spot market over 'One China' spat
World.content:
Taiwan has suspended some liquefied natural gas (LNG) purchases from Papua New Guinea as part of an escalating diplomatic dispute over the future of its representative office in Port Moresby.

But it has backed down from a threat to tear up a major gas contract with the Pacific nation.

PNG's Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko drew a furious response from Taipei earlier this month when he announced PNG would immediately shut Taiwan's de-facto embassy in "recognition" of his country's One China policy.

China has publicly celebrated the decision, with Foreign Minister Wang Yi declaring it could set a model for other nations, stirring anxieties in Taipei that other countries could follow suit, undermining its informal diplomatic network around the world.

Taiwan lodged a formal diplomatic protest in the wake of the announcement, saying the decision was made unilaterally, that Taipei would not accept it, and that its officials would stay at their post.

It also vowed to revise its gas contracts with PNG in response, including a long-term contract until 2030 to import 1.2 million tonnes of LNG every year.

PNG ousts Taiwan officials from the country Papua New Guinea will close Taiwan's trade mission in the country, in a major strategic move designed to reaffirm ties with China.

Taiwan has not touched that contract but yesterday a senior official from its foreign ministry announced it would suspend separate spot purchases on the open market.

It said that amounted to about 500,000 tonnes of LNG every six months.

Under current market rates, the sum appears to be worth about $800 million, although analysts say it could be worth more given volatility in gas markets.

But Graeme Smith from the Australian National University said he did not think the move would have a major financial impact on PNG, because it was likely to find other sellers quickly, partly because of the energy shocks caused by the Iran war and the chaos in the Strait of Hormuz.

"Because of what Trump is doing in Iran it's a bit of a sellers market for LNG so I don't think PNG will be too worried," he said.

" But it's essentially a way for Taiwan to make the statement that it's not happy. "

The Australian government has not commented publicly on the case, with multiple ministers saying last week that it was not for Canberra to weigh in on the sovereign decisions made by PNG.

But one Australian government source told the ABC that Taiwan was clearly trying to "remind" PNG that it remained an important trading partner, and to signal that it was not willing to accept the decision.

Taiwan has also threatened to review or cut its development programs in Papua New Guinea, although the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday said it was not yet taking that step.

Taiwan's official representatives have remained in PNG since the dispute broke out, and Papua New Guinea's government has not yet made any attempt to force them out.

Professor Smith said the "irony" was that PNG's decision to close the office was "in some ways, not really about Taiwan".

"It's about PNG sending a signal to China that despite its quite close security agreements with both Australia and the United States, that it still wants to be China's friend," he said.

" And Taiwan has been caught in the crossfire. "

The ABC has contacted PNG's Department of Foreign Affairs for comment.

World.title: Rugby Australia tight-lipped on possible Cheika homecoming
World.content:
Rugby Australia boss Phil Waugh has danced around the prospect of Michael Cheika's NSW Waratahs return as the search for a new coach narrows.

Dan McKellar stepped down with a year to run on his three-year deal, citing personal reasons, in a surprise development last month.

Expressions of interest for the vacancy closed last Friday.

It is understood former Waratahs and Wallabies coach Cheika, currently on a one-year deal as an assistant with the NRL's Sydney Roosters, has not yet applied for the role.

The Waratahs' high-performance program is run by Rugby Australia.

Cheika has coached Leicester Tigers, Argentina and the Lebanese rugby league team in recent years. (Getty Images: James Baylis)

Cheika was the first man to win major club titles in the Northern (Leinster in 2009) and Southern (Waratahs in 2014) Hemispheres and won World Rugby's 2015 coach of the year award.

Since his departure from the Waratahs in 2015, they have only played one semi-final, finishing eighth with a 5-9 record this year and struggling to build continuity in their roster.

Waugh refused to say if he had spoken to Cheika about the job, but was open to the prospect of his return to Australian rugby.

Stephen Hoiles, Chris Latham and John Manenti are also reportedly in the mix.

"We want world-class coaches, right across the system," Waugh said.

"That's our focus; there's multiple applicants, and we're working through it.

"We want to provide certainty to players and supporters as quickly as we can.

A schoolboy rugby 'dynasty' It might be more than 60 years ago, but Homebush Boys High's 1965 Waratah Shield win remains a fond memory for the likes of Gordon Bray, John Symond and John Coates.

"I don't like to anchor myself to timelines when it comes to coaching announcements, but we're conscious of getting the right person and the importance of a successful Waratahs in a World Cup year."

Waugh added RA would continue to discuss future opportunities with departed coach Joe Schmidt despite the New Zealander lining up work in Ireland as a consultant with Ulster, offering guidance to the province's age-grade coaches.

The role could reportedly see him make multiple visits, while he also committed to be part of the Australia A coaching set-up under Stephen Larkham.

Waugh on Wednesday said Schmidt was "free to do as he pleased" when asked if his return to Ireland had been flagged.

"We've got a very close relationship with Joe and are appreciative of his contribution," Waugh said.

"We'll continue conversations with how he can be involved and have been pretty open about that."

AAP

World.title: Drone captures rare video of 'magical moment' whale birth
World.content:
A drone operator has captured a rare sighting of a humpback whale giving birth on the New South Wales coast.

Drone pilot Alex Forrest is one of just four people to capture a whale giving birth, and the first to do so with a drone.

The Organisation for the Rescue and Research of Cetaceans in Australia (ORRCA) volunteer noticed the humpback whale swimming behind the pod, and began filming her from about 700 metres off the shore at Kingscliff on Tuesday afternoon.

"There was this one female whale going unusually slow, but she wasn't sleeping," he said.

" All of a sudden red just spurted out and there was a plumage; I was like, 'Is there an interaction with a predator?' "

"I had no idea until it reached the surface."

Alex Forrest captured the birth of a humpback whale on the New South Wales coast. (Supplied: ORRCA)

ORCCA said Mr Forrest filmed the whales at a distance of more than 100 metres in compliance with the NSW Biodiversity Conservation Regulation.

He has captured thousands of humpback whales from above, but he said the surprise was beyond belief.

"I hope this footage can contribute to the very little known about humpback whale birthing," Mr Forrest said.

Whale experts say the video will help with research into the field. (Supplied: ORRCA)

Macquarie University whale scientist Vanessa Pirotta said the sighting was an incredible moment.

"This is incredible. People watch humpback whales every single year, they're the world's most watched whale," Dr Pirotta said.

"This is a magical moment of an animal that could live up to 80-plus years.

"When your baby wants to come it'll come, the fact that baby knew exactly what to do which was to rise to the surface, was a very special moment."

Loading...

ORRCA said it believed it was the first drone recording of a humpback whale birth, and the fourth time the phenomenon had been filmed.

ORRCA head of research Annie Post said the footage would help to compare other documented whale births in the world.

The mother and calf were seen about 700 metres off Kingscliff on Tuesday. (Supplied: ORRCA)

"She seemed to be travelling alone and on her own when she gave birth, we can compare to others who have been escorted," she said.

Ms Post said the footage would be peer reviewed and contribute to knowledge on marine mammals.

"The more data we can collect, the more we can pick up on any trends," Ms Post said.

University of New South Wales PhD candidate Jane McPhee-Frew said the sighting differed to what was previously known about where humpback whales went to give birth.

"We had an idea they had to go to the tropics to give birth; we're sort of having to unlearn a little bit," she said.

Ms McPhee-Frew said the sighting was likely due to the growing population of humpback whales and the use of technology.

"It's building a picture of how animals and the environment change through space and time, how we think we have got something figured out but turns out there's a little bit more to it," she said.

World.title: Ben Carroll calls a royal commission, but critics await details
World.content:
New Victorian premier Ben Carroll has been at pains to distance himself from his predecessor Jacinta Allan in an attempt to revive Labor's hopes at the coming state election.

As part of the "new direction" he has promised, Mr Carroll has called a royal commission into the construction sector, something Ms Allan steadfastly refused to do in the final months of her leadership.

Mr Carroll said he met with the head of the Department of Premier and Cabinet yesterday and asked him to "get to work immediately" on the royal commission, which will investigate corruption in the multi-decade, $100 billion government construction project known as the "Big Build".

Serious allegations have been made of misconduct, corruption and violence on government worksites and estimates suggest Victorian taxpayers have lost up to $15 billion due to criminal activity.

But details are still scant on exactly what the royal commission will cover, leaving integrity experts and critics waiting for an indication of the full scope of the inquiry.

Premier promises 'exhaustive' investigation

Royal commissions are bound by terms of reference, which define what the inquiry should look at.

Ms Carroll says he wants "exhaustive terms of reference" that will leave no-one outside the scope of the investigation.

"I want no stone unturned, whether it is top-tier contractors, subcontractors, labour hire, government, unions," he said.

The announcement has been welcomed by integrity experts and agencies around the country.

Anti-corruption organisation Transparency International Australia says a forensic investigation of what has occurred on Big Build sites is the only way for the government to win back the trust of Victorians.

"Only a royal commission with broad terms of reference and strong coercive powers will truly uncover what went wrong, who was responsible and what needs to change," TIA chief executive Clancy Moore said.

"This is key for Premier Carroll to have any credibility with voters."

Anti-corruption barrister Geoffrey Watson SC, the author of a damning report exposing allegations of crime, corruption, violence and extortion within the Victorian branch of the CFMEU, said the announcement of the royal commission was "music to [his] ears".

Geoffrey Watson says the system what set up in a way that made it vulnerable to outside influences. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

He said there was something "radically" wrong with Victoria's enterprise bargaining agreement system and that the royal commission would uncover the full details.

Mr Watson said that system "concentrated the power in the hands of very few people".

"It made it susceptible to external corruption," he said.

Robert Redlich, the former commissioner of Victoria's Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission (IBAC), said the announcement was long overdue.

"We've needed one. This has been a historic public scandal unprecedented which demands something like a royal commission," he said.

"One has got to recognise that this huge public wastage means that money that could have gone to health, could have gone to education, to all sorts of other things, is missing.

"Ultimately Victorians will pay the price. Not just for this generation but the next generation to come from the fact that the debt has so grown."

Opposition slams 'sham' announcement

Mr Redlich said the effectiveness of the royal commission into construction would depend heavily on the terms of reference.

"There have been occasions when governments have called royal commissions, but given the royal commission very, very limited jurisdiction to investigate," he said.

The Victorian opposition is warning of that risk. Liberal leader Jess Wilson said what Mr Carroll had announced was a "fake royal commission".

"If Ben Carroll is serious about a real royal commission into the largest corruption in this state's history, of course it should be set up before the election," Ms Wilson said.

"But I suspect that we're going to have a sham royal commission without terms of reference that will ensure that we're calling witnesses from the Labor party, former ministers, current ministers."

Jess Wilson says the government has announced a "fake royal commission" that will not match one promised by the Coalition. (ABC News)

Ms Wilson has also called for Mr Carroll's predecessor to be called to give evidence before the royal commission.

"Jacinta Allan must be called to give evidence," she said.

"We know that Victorians want her to answer for how this has happened in the first place. She set up the system, she's the architect of the Big Build."

Mr Redlich said Ms Allan "undoubtedly" should be called, along with her predecessor, Daniel Andrews.

Mr Redlich said investigating how the CFMEU came to wield so much power on Big Build sites was something that only Mr Andrews could answer, because the project began under his premiership.

"If the royal commission is going to look at where the problems started, why they started, that's the place at which the royal commission must commence," Mr Redlich said.

World.title: ASX surges as slowing inflation lowers rate hike odds; CSL, Rio rally
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX surges as slowing inflation lowers rate hike odds; CSL, Rio rally Staff writers Updated July 29, 2026 — 5:56pm ,first published July 29, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket had a strong session on Wednesday as the nation’s latest inflation figures showed prices are not increasing as quickly as feared by the Reserve Bank, sharply reducing the chance of an interest rate rise at the bank’s August meeting. The S&P/ASX 200 finished 90.80 points, or 1 per cent higher, at 9038.60, having spiked 1.5 per cent immediately after the release of figures by the Australian Bureau of Statistics that showed annual headline inflation eased to 3.8 per cent in June. The bank had been expecting it to reach 4.8 per cent. The ASX surged higher on Wednesday. Oscar Colman The underlying measure of inflation – which seeks to take out extreme price increases and drops – was flat at 3.6 per cent, below the 3.7 per cent predicted by economists and the 3.8 per cent expected by the RBA. The central bank raised rates at its first three meetings of the year to try to suppress resurgent inflation pressures that emerged even before the US-Iran war triggered a fuel-price shock. Traders sharply wound back wagers on another rate hike this year to about 50 per cent, from more than 90 per cent before the release of the figures. The Australian dollar dipped 0.3 per cent to US69.54¢.



The data was “softer than we expected, and it was pretty nice to see some hot services categories ticking down in June”, said AMP economist My Bui. “It’s still high, though, so we still think there is potential for one more hike this year.” Related Article Updated

Inflation Big four banks put rate cuts back on the menu after surprising inflation drop CreditorWatch’s chief economist Ivan Colhoun said the data “eases the immediate pressure on the RBA to act”, though he still expects further modest tightening later in the year. Consumer and tech stocks – both cyclical sectors that would benefit from an end to rising interest rates – were up strongly after the release of the CPI data. Bunnings and Officeworks owner Wesfarmers rose 1.6 per cent, electronics retailer JB Hi-Fi jumped 4.7 per cent and Harvey Norman gained 4.1 per cent. Supermarket chains Woolworths and Coles added 1.9 per cent and 2.5 per cent, respectively, and Treasury Wine Estates gained 4.1 per cent. Software makers also rallied, pulling the tech sector higher. WiseTech Global gained 2.3 per cent, while Xero climbed 4.1 per cent and Technology One rose 3.4 per cent. Family tracking app Life 360 jumped 3.7 per cent. AI data centre operator NextDC, however, dropped 1.3 per cent.



Australia’s biggest pharma stock, CSL, soared 7.2 per cent after the biotech giant said that following talks with US and European regulators it will start clinical trials to finalise approvals for a new technology that would allow it to produce a higher immunoglobulin yield from plasma. Other healthcare stocks also advanced, with sleep apnoea devices maker Resmed up 3.6 per cent and Chemist Warehouse owner Sigma gaining 2.8 per cent. Rio Tinto shares climbed 3.7 per cent after the mining heavyweight said first-half profit soared as strong commodity prices outweighed the impact of China’s economic slowdown, US tariff campaigns and the conflict in the Middle East. The world’s second-biggest miner reported underlying profit of $US6.85 billion ($9.9 billion) for the half, 43 per cent above last year’s first half, beating analyst estimates of $US6.78 billion. Shares of its bigger rival BHP added 1.4 per cent, while Fortescue rose 2 per cent. Prices of iron ore – Rio’s biggest earner – remained steady over the six-month period, despite plateauing demand from dominant buyer China. The company is yet to complete negotiations with state-backed buyer China Mineral Resources Group over forward supply agreements. Rio continues to push its core growth strategy in copper, the metal key for the energy transition, with a ramp-up at its Oyu Tolgoi mine in Mongolia. Copper prices have climbed about 10 per cent this year, driven by supply disruptions and boost in demand from data centres.



Energy stocks were mixed, with oil and gas giant Woodside up 1.4 per cent and Santos flat as oil prices spiked yet again after a three-day slump. Related Article Energy Oil and gas giant becomes one of Australia’s biggest winners from Iran war Brent crude climbed almost 4 per cent to above $US87 a barrel, paring some of the 16 per cent loss over the past three sessions, which had been its biggest decline since 2020. The US military said it intercepted an Iranian “attempted surprise attack” on US troops based in the Middle East. Meanwhile, the US military and Saudi Arabia also struck “Iran-aligned terrorists” in Iraq after they were directed by the IRGC to target American forces and Saudi energy infrastructure, US Central Command said. Most of Wall Street rose overnight, even as stocks of computer chipmakers continued to tumble worldwide. The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent, but the modest move masked big swings underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537 points, or 1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after briefly dropping 9.3 per cent below its record set last month. On Wall Street, Apple became just the second company ever to achieve a $US5 trillion market valuation.



The iPhone maker’s shares rose as much as 1.8 per cent to $US342.89 early in the session, pushing the company’s market capitalisation to above $US5 trillion for the first time before falling back below the mark as shares eased before closing at $US340.80. Nvidia closed at a record $US5.7 trillion on May 14, but it has since lost about $US1 trillion in valuation. Apple is now the biggest company in the S&P 500 Index. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

Female police officer stabbed in neck

World.title: Struggling live music venues say nightlife plan will deliver big wins
World.content:
Liquor licensing discounts and incentives for local artists, proposed in reforms to Brisbane’s nightlife economy, could prevent dozens of small live music venues from closing, operators and stakeholders say, as many still struggle to recover from the pandemic. Operators told this masthead the changes would bring much-needed financial support for small venues while modernising the city’s live music scene, despite the rejection of more than 20 recommendations from the Night-Life Economy Commissioner’s report, published on Wednesday. Crowbar Brisbane chief executive Tyla Dombroski, whose venue replaced Fortitude Valley stalwart The Zoo in 2024, praised the Crisafulli government’s plan for recognising the importance of live music in driving the nighttime economy. Trad Nathan (left) and Tyla Dombroski (right) reopened Crowbar Brisbane on Ann Street after The Zoo closed in 2024. Crowbar Brisbane Initiatives proposed by the government include reviewing default sound limits, considering liquor licensing discounts for grassroots live music venues, modernising conditions for extended trading hours, and removing unnecessary red tape for licensees.



“It’s great and a really long time coming for Queensland,” Dombroski said. Related Article City life State rejects nightlife tsar’s push for extended retail, end to ID scans “There’s a lot of work that’s gone into it to work on ways to modernise and strengthen what live music venues can do and how they can operate with relaxed licensing laws and red tape.” She welcomed targeted relief for smaller venues, many of which have closed since the pandemic. “The large venues are usually part of a group, and they’ve got a lot more support and financial stability,” she said.



“These smaller venues are sometimes struggling week to week. We’re dealing with the constant issues of lower customer spending, increased operating costs, [and] liquor licence fees. “Encouraging local businesses to operate and have that nighttime economy increase is really important … especially with the Olympics coming in a few years.” QMusic supports Bigsound – one of the southern hemisphere’s largest music showcases – held in Fortitude Valley annually. Morgan Roberts John “JC” Collins, whose Moonside report contained 62 proposals to fix Brisbane’s nightlife, told the media earlier on Wednesday he was disappointed that some of the recommendations were not supported. But he planned to continue in his role, he said, advocating for faster implementation of the accepted recommendations, and lobbying for those not yet supported.



QMusic, a not-for-profit music industry peak body that receives funding from state and federal governments, applauded the plan’s support for local and emerging artists, and the reforms targeting grassroots venues that operate as the backbone of the city’s live music scene. Related Article Food ‘One uppercut after another’: Brisbane dining 2025 in review “Getting a Queensland artist on the bill for a stadium show is a career-changing opportunity, and the Homegrown initiative gives touring acts a real incentive to make that happen,” QMusic interim chief executive Kristy Ellis said. “Grassroots venues are where every Queensland artist gets their start. If those rooms disappear, the whole pipeline disappears with them. “Reducing barriers to putting on live music is one of the most important things for this industry, [and] we’re glad to see it prioritised.”



Joy owner Sarah Baldwin, whose restaurant in Bakery Lane is situated in the heart of the city’s busiest late-night precinct, supported the plan’s efforts to highlight a more diverse nighttime economy. But she said she was disappointed to see that recommendations for extended public transport – including a pilot program of trains between 1am and 4am on weekends – had been dismissed. “Any small step to making the Valley become a place that people can see as something that is an entertainment precinct, more than just clubbing and booze, is great,” Baldwin said. “The things like providing discounts to licensed venues that do have live music, that’s great. “But public transport not being extended? I feel like that doesn’t quite align.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Jewish patients discouraged from care by discriminatory doctors’ posts, regulator warns
World.content:
Discriminatory social media posts by doctors can discourage Jewish patients from seeking medical care, Australia’s health practitioner regulator has told the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency found social media was connected to between 40 and 45 per cent of racism or discrimination complaints. The figure rose to 85 per cent for those involving antisemitism or Islamophobia, according to the review conducted from October 2023 to the start of this year. AHPRA chief Justin Untersteiner outside the royal commission on Wednesday. James Brickwood Chief executive Justin Untersteiner said harmful posts could damage trust in the medical system. “It can actually lead to patients who need care not getting the care that they need,” he said.



AHPRA adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism in June after previously resisting it over free-speech concerns. Untersteiner said criticism of the Israeli government would not, by itself, constitute antisemitism. Doctors remained free to discuss political issues if they did so respectfully and accurately. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Patients requested Jewish identity be removed from medical documents, royal commission hears “But as soon as that veers into discrimination or racism, [they] would then certainly have the attention of us as a regulator,” he said. Untersteiner also said doctors “very rarely” could claim they were acting privately when posting on social media.



“There is a special relationship and a special level of trust that is placed in a health practitioner and a health system,” he said. “It becomes an artificial argument about whether someone is acting in a private or public capacity. The damage and the harm can be all the same.” University of Sydney academic Zhaoli Dai-Keller said some healthcare workers had become afraid to identify themselves as Jewish because of prejudice from colleagues and institutions. Jewish Medical Federation president Jack Green described “increased politicisation” in healthcare after the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023. Federation member Adam Gordon said some Jewish patients questioned whether they would receive impartial treatment, including while under anaesthetic.



“They’re under an anaesthetic and they’re worried about what’s going to happen to them,” Gordon said. Lawson Broad and Ben Bolot from JewishCare leave the royal commission in Sydney. James Brickwood JewishCare chief executive Lawson Broad said staff feared for their safety after a car was firebombed and defaced with antisemitic graffiti near its Woollahra office. Staff were concerned about coming to work, being visible through office windows and whether they could be shot, he said. JewishCare president Ben Bolot called for antisemitism to be recognised as a distinct category of trauma so victims were not repeatedly required to explain their experiences when seeking government support.



The evidence came as a global report found Australia recorded the largest rise in antisemitic incidents among the seven biggest Jewish communities outside Israel following the October 7 attacks. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission NSW Police reject Minns’ proposal to arm guards for public Jewish events Australian incidents increased by 246 per cent between 2022 and 2025, compared with 70 per cent in the United States and 123 per cent in the United Kingdom. Reports fell by 20 per cent over the past year, but Australia still recorded the second-highest rate in 2025, with 14 incidents for every 1000 Jewish residents. “The outlook for 2026 is not optimistic,” the J7 Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism said. World.title: Silver linings and blonde renewals: Why Wallabies enforcer stayed chilled about Schmidt snub
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Silver linings and blonde renewals: Why Wallabies enforcer stayed chilled about Schmidt snub Iain Payten July 29, 2026 — 5:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He tipped the scales at a bulked-up 140kg for the Reds this year and says “bully-ball” is part of the enforcer package he brings to any footy side. But Wallabies lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto says he still has the hops to be bankable lineout option as well, after winning a recall to the Australian squad under new coach Les Kiss. Wallabies player Lukhan Salakaia-Loto attends training. Audrey Richardson Salakaia-Loto returned to the Wallabies camp this week after being a contentious omission in Joe Schmidt’s last squad, for the July Test series against Ireland, France and Italy. Coming after a dominant season for the Reds, in which the 45-cap Wallaby was named in the Super Rugby team of the year, Salakaia-Loto’s omission continued a tense relationship with Schmidt where he was in and out of Wallabies squads, most notably when the big lock was overlooked for the British and Irish Lions series.



In explaining Salakaia-Loto’s absence for the July Tests, Schmidt questioned his physical condition, saying the lock had been inconsistent in games, and that he’d wanted “fast-jumping locks” for the Wallabies. Salakaia-Loto would use July “to get himself into the best physical shape to best contribute to the team,” Schmidt said. Salakaia-Loto said he had been disappointed to miss selection but, in keeping with the bemused social media posts he made at the time, the 29-year-old said he’d kept a sense of perspective. Wallabies player Lukhan Salakaia-Loto trains at the North Sydney Oval on Wednesday. Audrey Richardson “I’m used to it now,” Salakaia-Loto said of his Wallabies omission. “No, it was good, it was important for me to be home. “Two months ago, I just had my third daughter, so the silver lining for me was just spending time at home and being present with my kids, being able to wrestle the older two, give mum a bit of a break.



“It was a blessing in disguise. So [I was] disappointed, but there are more things to life than just being selected for a team.” Salakaia-Loto – whose new peroxided hairstyle was encouraged by his daughters – said he had taken the omission in his stride. “I did all I could do, so I was happy,” he said. “I was at peace with what I produced throughout the Super season, and you don’t always get what you deserve, I guess. You can’t dwell on it too much. So it’s nice to be named, but it doesn’t guarantee you anything.” Salakaia-Loto confirmed he had played at the heavier weight of 138kg for the Reds this season – up from a usual 132kg to 133kg – after arriving back from pre-season bigger, and finding the extra size helped on a physical front but not at the cost of reduced mobility and fitness.



“That was intentional, to be able to play the sort of style I wanted to play this year,” he said. “But I am lighter now after a good little block [of training] at Ballymore.” There was no specific mention of Schmidt but Salakaia-Loto was quick to point out his size had never impacted his lineout ability. “I’ve always been able to jump in the lineout, so no matter how, I can still get up there,” he said. Loading The aggressive lock was also quick to stress he did not expect to be rushed back into the Wallabies second row for the upcoming clashes with Japan, after Jeremy Williams and Reds teammate Josh Canham were outstanding in the Nations Championship Tests.



“‘Jez’ and Canham have done an unreal job, and I’m not expecting any change anytime soon,” Salakaia-Loto said. “It’s good to see Canham take big steps this year. He’s a real baller – he’s someone who’s got a massive future ahead of him.” Salakaia-Loto is also looking forward to training alongside Miles Amatosero, the combative young Waratahs lock with whom he has often butted heads in Super Rugby. “The best way of helping someone like Miles is pushing him and challenging him,” Salakaia-Loto said. “So iron sharpens iron. So I’m sure we’ll probably lock horns in training, but we know each other a bit more now on a personal level. He’s got all the potential in the world to be whatever he wants to be.” Meanwhile, Rugby Australia plans to use $15 million in federal government funding to increase female participation by 70 per cent – and overall participation by almost 40 per cent – by 2029. The funding is part of a $90 million Rugby World Cup package announced on Wednesday, which was pledged by the government in 2022 as part of Australia’s winning bid to host the 2027 men’s and 2029 women’s World Cups.



Related Article PNG Pocock warns NRL’s $600m PNG push risks undermining rugby in Fiji With $60 million going to World Rugby to help deliver the World Cups, a further $30 million in long-term legacy funding was granted under two “Beyond Impact” programs – one in Australia and one in the Pacific. The Australian program will focus on growing the game at community level and the Pacific funding will help support community and high-performance goals, particularly in the women’s game. It is separate from the $150 million, five-year Vaimoana program; the partnership being worked on by the Australian government to develop rugby in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga.

World.title: CCTV shows kindergarten runaways’ gleeful escape down major road
World.content:
Video has emerged of the moments after two young children managed to escape a childcare centre, with the pair seen running and skipping down the footpath by themselves. CCTV footage, obtained by Nine News, shows a little boy and girl gleefully making their way down St Georges Road in Fitzroy North just after 11am on Monday. CCTV footage shows two children running down the street after escaping from a Fitzroy North kindergarten on Monday. Nine News The girl, dressed in a purple top and pink pants, and the boy, wearing dark-coloured clothing, turn to look behind them as they pass strangers on the busy strip. Traffic on the road includes a tram, truck and multiple cars. Pedestrians on the street stop and turn when they see the pair run past. The escapees, aged four and five, walked more than a kilometre to one of the children’s homes after removing fencing from a playground garden at Isabel Henderson Kindergarten.



A concerned stranger followed the little girl and little boy as they walked down the busy road, said a woman with knowledge of the incident, but who asked not to be identified to protect the families’ privacy. The good Samaritan directed another stranger to call the police and continued to track the children to one of their homes after the pair ignored her requests to stop. Two children escaped from a kindergarten in Melbourne’s inner north on Monday, prompting an investigation into the safety of the early learning facility’s playground. Ruby Alexander The family of one of the children was home at the time and let them in to watch television while the centre and police were called. The kids reportedly sat down to watch KPop Demon Hunters, an animated musical fantasy film. The Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority was investigating the incident on Tuesday.



A spokesperson said the regulator would not hesitate to take strong action to protect children’s safety. Related Article Early childhood Children escaped kindergarten through playground fence, went home, watched TV Kindergarten director Anna Tibb on Tuesday said the centre had launched an internal investigation into the matter and was working with the management committee and relevant authorities. “This is really devastating for the families involved and for us,” Tibb said. “We are a very transparent and open organisation, and we take these things very seriously.” The centre installed temporary fencing in a section of the kindergarten playground after it was discovered that the children had escaped by removing the brush fencing, an outdoor barrier made from tightly packed brush or branches.



In a letter to parents, Tibb said she would be speaking to the children about safety on Tuesday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: One faulty fan gridlocked thousands of hapless commuters on the M5
World.content:
In a global city such as Sydney, a place where people want to live and work, it will never be possible to prevent congestion. But the major traffic delays experienced by motorists during the morning peak on Sydney’s M5 motorway while a tunnel ventilator fan was repaired could fairly be described as a commuting catastrophe.

The tunnel on the M5 motorway was closed for more than six hours on Wednesday, and city-bound traffic backed up more than 13 kilometres at times as crew with cranes worked to fix the fan.

The toll road operator, Transurban, had closed the two-lane tunnel to conduct routine maintenance in the early hours of Wednesday when workers discovered safety problems with a fan inside the tunnel. A decision was made on safety grounds about 4.16am to replace the fan and keep the eastbound lanes shut after 5am, despite the looming morning peak.

Traffic came to a standstill on the M5 on Wednesday morning. Nine News

It was the latest episode in the saga of the M5 East Tunnel, a vital part of Sydney’s infrastructure that has been plagued by operational problems almost from the start. The project was completed on a tight budget and under an aggressive schedule in 2001 and was soon bedevilled by repeated shutdowns – accidents, flooding and computer glitches. And so it went. Only a year ago, a crane rolled in the eastbound tunnel, and it was shut for nearly 24 hours.

World.title: Demand for toll refunds after seven-hour Sydney motorway closure causes chaos
World.content:
Australia’s largest toll road operator is facing demands to refund motorists caught in hours-long delays on Wednesday morning caused by the closure of one of the M5 motorway tunnels to replace a faulty fan. Transurban kept the 25-year-old eastbound tunnel closed until shortly before noon – seven hours longer than planned – while workers replaced the fan, causing traffic to queue as far as 13 kilometres to Milperra during the morning peak. Traffic came to a standstill on the M5. Nine News Premier Chris Minns said the closure had thrown many people’s commute into chaos, and the roads minister would seek answers from Transurban about its maintenance schedule and the chances of a repeat incident. “I know that’s cold comfort for people that were stuck in traffic this morning. I’m genuinely sorry about that,” Minns said. “It’s not good enough.”



Transurban earns about half of its annual $3.73 billion revenue from the 11 toll roads – including the M5 – it controls in Sydney. The Sydney Harbour Bridge and Harbour Tunnel are the city’s only toll roads that are not controlled by Australia’s largest private operator. Traffic counts indicate nearly 10,000 motorists travel eastbound through the M5 tunnel on Wednesday mornings. Coalition roads spokesman Mark Coure called on Transurban to immediately refund every toll paid by motorists caught in the M5 chaos. “Thousands of people paid to use what should be a reliable motorway, only to be left sitting in gridlock for hours. Motorists should not be forced to pay for a service they simply did not receive,” he said.



The opposition also demanded the government declare a toll-free travel day on the M5 to compensate motorists for the disruption. Cars are charged a maximum of $9.15 to use the M5 East between Beverly Hills and Mascot, while trucks are tolled $27.47. The M5 East is part of WestConnex and has distance-based tolls, unlike the connecting M5 Southwest, on which cars are charged $6.06 regardless of the journey length. Motoring group NRMA said Transurban should consider providing toll refunds on a case-by-case basis to motorists disrupted by the tunnel closure. “We have more tunnels in Sydney than ever before and more are coming online. The onus is on the government and the toll road operators to work together to minimise these severe disruptions,” spokesperson Peter Khoury said.



Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said any decision regarding toll refunds was a matter for the operator, noting that the decision to close the tunnel was made on safety grounds. Related Article Roads Motorists stuck in Sydney’s M4 tunnel for hours after bulges found in roof “We acknowledge Wednesday morning was frustrating for motorists and understand the disruption caused,” she said. The toll road operator had closed the M5 tunnel to conduct routine maintenance from 9.30pm on Tuesday to 5am on Wednesday when workers discovered safety problems with a ventilator fan inside the tunnel. A decision was made on safety grounds at 4.16am to replace the fan and keep the eastbound lanes shut after 5am, despite the looming morning peak. Two cranes and other equipment were called in for workers to replace the fan, which is one of 147 in the eastbound tunnel.



Transurban’s general manager for WestConnex, Denise Kelly, said the company encouraged any motorists who experienced significant delays to contact its toll-payment system Linkt to discuss refunds. She apologised to motorists for the major delays caused by the closure, but said the immediate priority on Wednesday had been safely removing the faulty jet fan and reopening the road for motorists by the afternoon peak. “We evaluated it to see whether or not it could be fixed in situ while it stayed up in the roof cavity. That was decided not to be the best course of action, and the best course of action was actually to remove it,” she said. She texted Aitchison at 4.42am to inform her of the decision to replace the fan and keep the tunnel closed, and the pair later spoke.



Kelly confirmed that Transurban was aware at the time of its decision that the tunnel would have to remain closed during the morning peak. Related Article Roads Sydney toll shake-up deadline missed as motorway charges rise again “That was the immediate advice to the minister and to the traffic management centre … that it would be closed for the morning peak,” she said. “We made that call very early, adjusted all of the signs and messaging, and put messaging out on links.” Transurban is still assessing what caused the faulty fan. Earlier, Transport for NSW coordinator-general Howard Collins had urged commuters to avoid the motorway “at all costs” due to the emergency works forcing the closure of the city-bound lanes of the M5 between King Georges Road in Beverly Hills and Marsh Street in Mascot.



In December, motorists were stuck in one of the city’s M4 motorway tunnels for hours after a major disruption was caused by two bulges found in the roof of the westbound tunnel beneath Ashfield in the inner west.
