World.title: ASX surges as slowing inflation lowers rate hike odds; CSL, Rio rally
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX surges as slowing inflation lowers rate hike odds; CSL, Rio rally Staff writers Updated July 29, 2026 — 5:56pm ,first published July 29, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket had a strong session on Wednesday as the nation’s latest inflation figures showed prices are not increasing as quickly as feared by the Reserve Bank, sharply reducing the chance of an interest rate rise at the bank’s August meeting. The S&P/ASX 200 finished 90.80 points, or 1 per cent higher, at 9038.60, having spiked 1.5 per cent immediately after the release of figures by the Australian Bureau of Statistics that showed annual headline inflation eased to 3.8 per cent in June. The bank had been expecting it to reach 4.8 per cent. The ASX surged higher on Wednesday. Oscar Colman The underlying measure of inflation – which seeks to take out extreme price increases and drops – was flat at 3.6 per cent, below the 3.7 per cent predicted by economists and the 3.8 per cent expected by the RBA. The central bank raised rates at its first three meetings of the year to try to suppress resurgent inflation pressures that emerged even before the US-Iran war triggered a fuel-price shock. Traders sharply wound back wagers on another rate hike this year to about 50 per cent, from more than 90 per cent before the release of the figures. The Australian dollar dipped 0.3 per cent to US69.54¢.



The data was “softer than we expected, and it was pretty nice to see some hot services categories ticking down in June”, said AMP economist My Bui. “It’s still high, though, so we still think there is potential for one more hike this year.” Related Article Updated

Inflation Big four banks put rate cuts back on the menu after surprising inflation drop CreditorWatch’s chief economist Ivan Colhoun said the data “eases the immediate pressure on the RBA to act”, though he still expects further modest tightening later in the year. Consumer and tech stocks – both cyclical sectors that would benefit from an end to rising interest rates – were up strongly after the release of the CPI data. Bunnings and Officeworks owner Wesfarmers rose 1.6 per cent, electronics retailer JB Hi-Fi jumped 4.7 per cent and Harvey Norman gained 4.1 per cent. Supermarket chains Woolworths and Coles added 1.9 per cent and 2.5 per cent, respectively, and Treasury Wine Estates gained 4.1 per cent. Software makers also rallied, pulling the tech sector higher. WiseTech Global gained 2.3 per cent, while Xero climbed 4.1 per cent and Technology One rose 3.4 per cent. Family tracking app Life 360 jumped 3.7 per cent. AI data centre operator NextDC, however, dropped 1.3 per cent.



Australia’s biggest pharma stock, CSL, soared 7.2 per cent after the biotech giant said that following talks with US and European regulators it will start clinical trials to finalise approvals for a new technology that would allow it to produce a higher immunoglobulin yield from plasma. Other healthcare stocks also advanced, with sleep apnoea devices maker Resmed up 3.6 per cent and Chemist Warehouse owner Sigma gaining 2.8 per cent. Rio Tinto shares climbed 3.7 per cent after the mining heavyweight said first-half profit soared as strong commodity prices outweighed the impact of China’s economic slowdown, US tariff campaigns and the conflict in the Middle East. The world’s second-biggest miner reported underlying profit of $US6.85 billion ($9.9 billion) for the half, 43 per cent above last year’s first half, beating analyst estimates of $US6.78 billion. Shares of its bigger rival BHP added 1.4 per cent, while Fortescue rose 2 per cent. Prices of iron ore – Rio’s biggest earner – remained steady over the six-month period, despite plateauing demand from dominant buyer China. The company is yet to complete negotiations with state-backed buyer China Mineral Resources Group over forward supply agreements. Rio continues to push its core growth strategy in copper, the metal key for the energy transition, with a ramp-up at its Oyu Tolgoi mine in Mongolia. Copper prices have climbed about 10 per cent this year, driven by supply disruptions and boost in demand from data centres.



Energy stocks were mixed, with oil and gas giant Woodside up 1.4 per cent and Santos flat as oil prices spiked yet again after a three-day slump. Related Article Energy Oil and gas giant becomes one of Australia’s biggest winners from Iran war Brent crude climbed almost 4 per cent to above $US87 a barrel, paring some of the 16 per cent loss over the past three sessions, which had been its biggest decline since 2020. The US military said it intercepted an Iranian “attempted surprise attack” on US troops based in the Middle East. Meanwhile, the US military and Saudi Arabia also struck “Iran-aligned terrorists” in Iraq after they were directed by the IRGC to target American forces and Saudi energy infrastructure, US Central Command said. Most of Wall Street rose overnight, even as stocks of computer chipmakers continued to tumble worldwide. The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent, but the modest move masked big swings underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537 points, or 1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after briefly dropping 9.3 per cent below its record set last month. On Wall Street, Apple became just the second company ever to achieve a $US5 trillion market valuation.



The iPhone maker’s shares rose as much as 1.8 per cent to $US342.89 early in the session, pushing the company’s market capitalisation to above $US5 trillion for the first time before falling back below the mark as shares eased before closing at $US340.80. Nvidia closed at a record $US5.7 trillion on May 14, but it has since lost about $US1 trillion in valuation. Apple is now the biggest company in the S&P 500 Index. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Struggling live music venues say nightlife plan will deliver big wins
World.content:
Liquor licensing discounts and incentives for local artists, proposed in reforms to Brisbane’s nightlife economy, could prevent dozens of small live music venues from closing, operators and stakeholders say, as many still struggle to recover from the pandemic. Operators told this masthead the changes would bring much-needed financial support for small venues while modernising the city’s live music scene, despite the rejection of more than 20 recommendations from the Night-Life Economy Commissioner’s report, published on Wednesday. Crowbar Brisbane chief executive Tyla Dombroski, whose venue replaced Fortitude Valley stalwart The Zoo in 2024, praised the Crisafulli government’s plan for recognising the importance of live music in driving the nighttime economy. Trad Nathan (left) and Tyla Dombroski (right) reopened Crowbar Brisbane on Ann Street after The Zoo closed in 2024. Crowbar Brisbane Initiatives proposed by the government include reviewing default sound limits, considering liquor licensing discounts for grassroots live music venues, modernising conditions for extended trading hours, and removing unnecessary red tape for licensees.



“It’s great and a really long time coming for Queensland,” Dombroski said. Related Article City life State rejects nightlife tsar’s push for extended retail, end to ID scans “There’s a lot of work that’s gone into it to work on ways to modernise and strengthen what live music venues can do and how they can operate with relaxed licensing laws and red tape.” She welcomed targeted relief for smaller venues, many of which have closed since the pandemic. “The large venues are usually part of a group, and they’ve got a lot more support and financial stability,” she said.



“These smaller venues are sometimes struggling week to week. We’re dealing with the constant issues of lower customer spending, increased operating costs, [and] liquor licence fees. “Encouraging local businesses to operate and have that nighttime economy increase is really important … especially with the Olympics coming in a few years.” QMusic supports Bigsound – one of the southern hemisphere’s largest music showcases – held in Fortitude Valley annually. Morgan Roberts John “JC” Collins, whose Moonside report contained 62 proposals to fix Brisbane’s nightlife, told the media earlier on Wednesday he was disappointed that some of the recommendations were not supported. But he planned to continue in his role, he said, advocating for faster implementation of the accepted recommendations, and lobbying for those not yet supported.



QMusic, a not-for-profit music industry peak body that receives funding from state and federal governments, applauded the plan’s support for local and emerging artists, and the reforms targeting grassroots venues that operate as the backbone of the city’s live music scene. Related Article Food ‘One uppercut after another’: Brisbane dining 2025 in review “Getting a Queensland artist on the bill for a stadium show is a career-changing opportunity, and the Homegrown initiative gives touring acts a real incentive to make that happen,” QMusic interim chief executive Kristy Ellis said. “Grassroots venues are where every Queensland artist gets their start. If those rooms disappear, the whole pipeline disappears with them. “Reducing barriers to putting on live music is one of the most important things for this industry, [and] we’re glad to see it prioritised.”



Joy owner Sarah Baldwin, whose restaurant in Bakery Lane is situated in the heart of the city’s busiest late-night precinct, supported the plan’s efforts to highlight a more diverse nighttime economy. But she said she was disappointed to see that recommendations for extended public transport – including a pilot program of trains between 1am and 4am on weekends – had been dismissed. “Any small step to making the Valley become a place that people can see as something that is an entertainment precinct, more than just clubbing and booze, is great,” Baldwin said. “The things like providing discounts to licensed venues that do have live music, that’s great. “But public transport not being extended? I feel like that doesn’t quite align.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Coming after a dominant season for the Reds, in which the 45-cap Wallaby was named in the Super Rugby team of the year, Salakaia-Loto’s omission continued a tense relationship with Schmidt where he was in and out of Wallabies squads, most notably when the big lock was overlooked for the British and Irish Lions series.

Salakaia-Loto would use July “to get himself into the best physical shape to best contribute to the team,” Schmidt said. Salakaia-Loto said he had been disappointed to miss selection but, in keeping with the bemused social media posts he made at the time, the 29-year-old said he’d kept a sense of perspective. Wallabies player Lukhan Salakaia-Loto trains at the North Sydney Oval on Wednesday. Audrey Richardson “I’m used to it now,” Salakaia-Loto said of his Wallabies omission. “No, it was good, it was important for me to be home. “Two months ago, I just had my third daughter, so the silver lining for me was just spending time at home and being present with my kids, being able to wrestle the older two, give mum a bit of a break.



“It was a blessing in disguise. So [I was] disappointed, but there are more things to life than just being selected for a team.” Salakaia-Loto – whose new peroxided hairstyle was encouraged by his daughters – said he had taken the omission in his stride. “I did all I could do, so I was happy,” he said. “I was at peace with what I produced throughout the Super season, and you don’t always get what you deserve, I guess. You can’t dwell on it too much. So it’s nice to be named, but it doesn’t guarantee you anything.” Salakaia-Loto confirmed he had played at the heavier weight of 138kg for the Reds this season – up from a usual 132kg to 133kg – after arriving back from pre-season bigger, and finding the extra size helped on a physical front but not at the cost of reduced mobility and fitness.



“That was intentional, to be able to play the sort of style I wanted to play this year,” he said. “But I am lighter now after a good little block [of training] at Ballymore.” There was no specific mention of Schmidt but Salakaia-Loto was quick to point out his size had never impacted his lineout ability. “I’ve always been able to jump in the lineout, so no matter how, I can still get up there,” he said. Loading The aggressive lock was also quick to stress he did not expect to be rushed back into the Wallabies second row for the upcoming clashes with Japan, after Jeremy Williams and Reds teammate Josh Canham were outstanding in the Nations Championship Tests.



“‘Jez’ and Canham have done an unreal job, and I’m not expecting any change anytime soon,” Salakaia-Loto said. “It’s good to see Canham take big steps this year. He’s a real baller – he’s someone who’s got a massive future ahead of him.” Salakaia-Loto is also looking forward to training alongside Miles Amatosero, the combative young Waratahs lock with whom he has often butted heads in Super Rugby. “The best way of helping someone like Miles is pushing him and challenging him,” Salakaia-Loto said. “So iron sharpens iron. So I’m sure we’ll probably lock horns in training, but we know each other a bit more now on a personal level. He’s got all the potential in the world to be whatever he wants to be.” Meanwhile, Rugby Australia plans to use $15 million in federal government funding to increase female participation by 70 per cent – and overall participation by almost 40 per cent – by 2029. The funding is part of a $90 million Rugby World Cup package announced on Wednesday, which was pledged by the government in 2022 as part of Australia’s winning bid to host the 2027 men’s and 2029 women’s World Cups.



Related Article PNG Pocock warns NRL’s $600m PNG push risks undermining rugby in Fiji With $60 million going to World Rugby to help deliver the World Cups, a further $30 million in long-term legacy funding was granted under two “Beyond Impact” programs – one in Australia and one in the Pacific. The Australian program will focus on growing the game at community level and the Pacific funding will help support community and high-performance goals, particularly in the women’s game. It is separate from the $150 million, five-year Vaimoana program; the partnership being worked on by the Australian government to develop rugby in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga.

World.title: CCTV shows kindergarten runaways’ gleeful escape down major road
World.content:
Video has emerged of the moments after two young children managed to escape a childcare centre, with the pair seen running and skipping down the footpath by themselves. CCTV footage, obtained by Nine News, shows a little boy and girl gleefully making their way down St Georges Road in Fitzroy North just after 11am on Monday. CCTV footage shows two children running down the street after escaping from a Fitzroy North kindergarten on Monday. Nine News The girl, dressed in a purple top and pink pants, and the boy, wearing dark-coloured clothing, turn to look behind them as they pass strangers on the busy strip. Traffic on the road includes a tram, truck and multiple cars. Pedestrians on the street stop and turn when they see the pair run past. The escapees, aged four and five, walked more than a kilometre to one of the children’s homes after removing fencing from a playground garden at Isabel Henderson Kindergarten.



A concerned stranger followed the little girl and little boy as they walked down the busy road, said a woman with knowledge of the incident, but who asked not to be identified to protect the families’ privacy. The good Samaritan directed another stranger to call the police and continued to track the children to one of their homes after the pair ignored her requests to stop. Two children escaped from a kindergarten in Melbourne’s inner north on Monday, prompting an investigation into the safety of the early learning facility’s playground. Ruby Alexander The family of one of the children was home at the time and let them in to watch television while the centre and police were called. The kids reportedly sat down to watch KPop Demon Hunters, an animated musical fantasy film. The Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority was investigating the incident on Tuesday.



A spokesperson said the regulator would not hesitate to take strong action to protect children’s safety. Related Article Early childhood Children escaped kindergarten through playground fence, went home, watched TV Kindergarten director Anna Tibb on Tuesday said the centre had launched an internal investigation into the matter and was working with the management committee and relevant authorities. “This is really devastating for the families involved and for us,” Tibb said. “We are a very transparent and open organisation, and we take these things very seriously.” The centre installed temporary fencing in a section of the kindergarten playground after it was discovered that the children had escaped by removing the brush fencing, an outdoor barrier made from tightly packed brush or branches.



In a letter to parents, Tibb said she would be speaking to the children about safety on Tuesday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Demand for toll refunds after seven-hour Sydney motorway closure causes chaos
World.content:
Australia’s largest toll road operator is facing demands to refund motorists caught in hours-long delays on Wednesday morning caused by the closure of one of the M5 motorway tunnels to replace a faulty fan. Transurban kept the 25-year-old eastbound tunnel closed until shortly before noon – seven hours longer than planned – while workers replaced the fan, causing traffic to queue as far as 13 kilometres to Milperra during the morning peak. Traffic came to a standstill on the M5. Nine News Premier Chris Minns said the closure had thrown many people’s commute into chaos, and the roads minister would seek answers from Transurban about its maintenance schedule and the chances of a repeat incident. “I know that’s cold comfort for people that were stuck in traffic this morning. I’m genuinely sorry about that,” Minns said. “It’s not good enough.”



Transurban earns about half of its annual $3.73 billion revenue from the 11 toll roads – including the M5 – it controls in Sydney. The Sydney Harbour Bridge and Harbour Tunnel are the city’s only toll roads that are not controlled by Australia’s largest private operator. Traffic counts indicate nearly 10,000 motorists travel eastbound through the M5 tunnel on Wednesday mornings. Coalition roads spokesman Mark Coure called on Transurban to immediately refund every toll paid by motorists caught in the M5 chaos. “Thousands of people paid to use what should be a reliable motorway, only to be left sitting in gridlock for hours. Motorists should not be forced to pay for a service they simply did not receive,” he said.



The opposition also demanded the government declare a toll-free travel day on the M5 to compensate motorists for the disruption. Cars are charged a maximum of $9.15 to use the M5 East between Beverly Hills and Mascot, while trucks are tolled $27.47. The M5 East is part of WestConnex and has distance-based tolls, unlike the connecting M5 Southwest, on which cars are charged $6.06 regardless of the journey length. Motoring group NRMA said Transurban should consider providing toll refunds on a case-by-case basis to motorists disrupted by the tunnel closure. “We have more tunnels in Sydney than ever before and more are coming online. The onus is on the government and the toll road operators to work together to minimise these severe disruptions,” spokesperson Peter Khoury said.



Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said any decision regarding toll refunds was a matter for the operator, noting that the decision to close the tunnel was made on safety grounds. Related Article Roads Motorists stuck in Sydney’s M4 tunnel for hours after bulges found in roof “We acknowledge Wednesday morning was frustrating for motorists and understand the disruption caused,” she said. The toll road operator had closed the M5 tunnel to conduct routine maintenance from 9.30pm on Tuesday to 5am on Wednesday when workers discovered safety problems with a ventilator fan inside the tunnel. A decision was made on safety grounds at 4.16am to replace the fan and keep the eastbound lanes shut after 5am, despite the looming morning peak. Two cranes and other equipment were called in for workers to replace the fan, which is one of 147 in the eastbound tunnel.



Transurban’s general manager for WestConnex, Denise Kelly, said the company encouraged any motorists who experienced significant delays to contact its toll-payment system Linkt to discuss refunds. She apologised to motorists for the major delays caused by the closure, but said the immediate priority on Wednesday had been safely removing the faulty jet fan and reopening the road for motorists by the afternoon peak. “We evaluated it to see whether or not it could be fixed in situ while it stayed up in the roof cavity. That was decided not to be the best course of action, and the best course of action was actually to remove it,” she said. She texted Aitchison at 4.42am to inform her of the decision to replace the fan and keep the tunnel closed, and the pair later spoke.



Kelly confirmed that Transurban was aware at the time of its decision that the tunnel would have to remain closed during the morning peak. Related Article Roads Sydney toll shake-up deadline missed as motorway charges rise again “That was the immediate advice to the minister and to the traffic management centre … that it would be closed for the morning peak,” she said. “We made that call very early, adjusted all of the signs and messaging, and put messaging out on links.” Transurban is still assessing what caused the faulty fan. Earlier, Transport for NSW coordinator-general Howard Collins had urged commuters to avoid the motorway “at all costs” due to the emergency works forcing the closure of the city-bound lanes of the M5 between King Georges Road in Beverly Hills and Marsh Street in Mascot.



In December, motorists were stuck in one of the city’s M4 motorway tunnels for hours after a major disruption was caused by two bulges found in the roof of the westbound tunnel beneath Ashfield in the inner west. World.title: Widdup team chasing more Grange success on Thursday

Trainer Brad Widdup. Getty

World.title: Police 'hold serious concerns' for missing 69-year-old in Auckland
World.content:
Police have serious concerns for a 69-year-old reported missing from a residential complex on Auckland's North Shore.

Maree Jennins was reported missing from the complex on Roseberry Rd in Birkenhead on Tuesday evening.

The last confirmed sighting of Jennins was on the afternoon of Friday, July 24.

She had no form of transport, but had been known to use taxis in the past, police said.

"We have made enquiries with taxi firms throughout the day, we know that Maree has recently avoided using her name when she has made taxi bookings. She may have caught a taxi from the Roseberry Rd or wider Birkenhead area," Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams, from Waitematā East CIB, said.

"Maree's family and police hold serious concerns for her following recent comments she has made. She stayed in a north Auckland motel recently and it is possible she has done the same again, but we continue to be worried for her wellbeing."

Police want any taxi drivers that might have picked her up on Friday afternoon to contact them. They have asked accommodation providers with information to get in touch as well.

Residents in the wider Birkenhead area that may have seen her should also contact police. Anyone who sees her should call 111 immediately.

World.title: Stillborn boy discovered on side of Marlborough road laid to rest
World.content:
A stillborn boy discovered on the side of the road in Marlborough has been laid to rest at a public funeral service.

About 30 people gathered this morning to mark the life of the boy, called Baby Doe, who was found by a mowing contractor on Wairau Bar Road on 19 May.

An investigation was launched, but police have not yet been able to identify the child or its family.

Funeral held for stillborn baby found on Marlborough roadside Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Baby Doe was laid to rest in a small white casket adorned with flowers, beneath an unnamed memorial plaque that read: "Every life that ever forms, touches the world in some small way, for all eternity."

The service was held at the children's memorial area at Fairhall Cemetery, near Blenheim.

The funeral service for Baby Doe at Fairhall Cemetery, near Blenheim, was attended by police, iwi and members of the public. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Police chaplain John Etheredge, who led the service, said while the circumstances were "tragic and traumatic", it was important to show love and respect for the young life.

"It will bring closure to those that are involved in it to a degree and it also puts it out there to hopefully to the mother and her family that people are caring about her."

He said many in the community had gone out of their way to show support for the baby and its family.

"We don't know what's happened with mum and how much agony it was to go through and to to lose the child, that must be terrible and quite traumatic," Etheredge said.

Wairau Bar Road, where the infant's body was found. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Iwi, police and members of the public were at the service, with some travelling from Nelson to mark their respects.

Ngāti Rārua representative Barney Thomas said a karakia and told those gathered: "This is our baby, belongs to all of us."

Detective Sergeant Jason Hillgrove said the baby was near full-term when he was stillborn, he appeared to have been cared for and was wrapped up when he was found.

"We've been endeavouring to try and identify who the mother is because our main concern through this investigation is to make sure that she's okay.

"We would really love to find out who she is so we can put a name to the baby, but also make sure that her welfare and mental health is looked after."

Detective Hannah McCabe and Detective Constable Paul Beckett, who were among the first on the scene, lower Baby Doe's casket at his funeral service. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Hillgrove said not knowing the boy's identity raised questions over how to appropriately lay him to rest.

"With the help of Sowman's [Funerals], the decision was made that we really need to have a service to allow the community to come together in grief for this little baby."

Two of the police officers first on the scene - Detective Hannah McCabe and Detective Constable Paul Beckett - also travelled with the baby to its post mortem in Christchurch, and Beckett read a poem at the service, before lowering the casket into the ground.

"Most of the police involved in this inquiry, we're parents too, so we've all been touched by this," Hillgrove said.

"This baby did belong to someone for nine months and that's the person we really want to find."

Iwi, police and members of the public at a funeral service for the stillborn baby found on Wairau Bar Road on 19 May, that has not yet been identified. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Marlborough mayor Nadine Taylor said it was important to honour Baby Doe in a proper memorial service.

"Somewhere there's a mother and a family, a whanau that's grieving for the loss of this baby and it was important that we came together as a community to be here on behalf of that family and to acknowledge Baby Doe."

Sowman's Funerals donated its time to make the service happen, with Mayflower Studio donating flowers and Artisan Memorials donating the plaque.

"Many parts of the community have contributed to this service, come together to make sure that the funeral is as it should be, is as it would be for any other much loved baby and that's been really important to the Marlborough community."

A plaque on the grave of Baby Doe, a stillborn boy discovered on the side of the Wairau Bar Road in Marlborough, on 19 May. RNZ / Samantha Gee

The plot at Fairhall Cemetery was donated by the Marlborough District Council, with Baby Doe buried among other children.

Sowman's Funerals manager Chelsea Brown said it was important that the baby had a final resting place, with a simple plaque, that people were able to visit.

"It's someone's baby and it's a life that needs to be represented."

Flowers from the Children's Commissioner on the grave of the stillborn baby found in Marlborough, named Baby Doe. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Flowers sent by the Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad were also placed on the grave.

"Tēnā koe pēpi, moe mai rā, moe mai rā, moe mai rā," the card attached to them read.

"Although you didn't have the chance to experience this world, we mourn for you, and will remember you, and we send our love to your māmā.

"Rest now, with the stars."

World.title: Overhauled Dog Control Act to be 'in place next year'
World.content:
An updated Dog Control Act should be in place by next year, Local Government Minister Simon Watts says.

On Wednesday he released guidelines which replace the guidance developed in 2009 and supplemented in 2015.

They were intended to help councils make full use of the tools currently available to them, promote responsible dog ownership and respond effectively when problems arose, Watts said,

Councils told to record more consistent data to tackle roaming dogs Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

He told Checkpoint it was the first phase of the comprehensive review of the Act ordered in March.

Too many Kiwis had been victims of dog attacks, "and we've even had loss of life", he said.

"We're aiming to have our recommendations to enable us to take steps to legislate by the end of this year, and have that law in place next year."

The guidelines also included standardised reporting across councils to "improve data collection", Watts added.

"Better information will help build a clearer picture of dog control issues across New Zealand and support better decision-making."

Local Government Minister Simon Watts RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Watts said standardised reporting was needed to guide the Dog Control Act, as it was difficult to review and change the legislation without it, but it was not yet mandatory.

"The consideration around the mandatory nature of whether this will be required formally will be something that we're considering through the legislation review that we're undertaking at the moment."

ACC recorded more than 14,000 claims related to dog bites and attacks in 2025.

World.title: Public service boss tells union to pull 'change the government' postcards from workplaces
World.content:
The country's top public servant has directed the Public Service Association (PSA) to stop handing out its "change the government" campaign material in departments and agencies, saying it breaches expectations of political neutrality.

But the union said that's an overreaction and is seeking an "urgent meeting" to make its case to the public service boss.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche wrote to the PSA on Wednesday that he had received "a number of queries" from public servants and union delegates about the campaign.

The country's top public servant has directed the Public Service Association to stop handing out its "change the government" campaign material. Supplied / PSA

He said the postcards were "clearly election advertising", noting they even included a promoter statement with the advertiser's name and contact details - a legal requirement for all election s.

Sir Brian said, as such, sharing or displaying them in public service workplaces breached the requirement for the sector to be politically neutral at all times.

"Public servants and the public service need to be kept safe from any accusations around political neutrality," he said.

"I am disappointed that public servants have been put in the unacceptable position where they have been asked to display and distribute material clearly inconsistent with our guidance."

In an email in response, PSA national secretaries Fleur Fitzsimons and Duane Leo said they disagreed that the postcards amounted to election advertising.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons disagreed that the union's postcards amounted to election advertising. Supplied

"It is important that public service agencies do not over-compensate during this time and unnecessarily restrict the right of public servants and their unions to express their views," they wrote.

The union asked Roche to refrain from briefing chief executives until the two sides had met and said it was seeking further legal advice.

RNZ, however, has seen an email already sent by Sir Brian to agencies notifying them of his decision and advising leaders to act in a "reasonable, fair and proportionate manner" if they needed to remove any advertising from their workplaces.

In his initial letter to the PSA, Roche said unions could still communicate with their members outside the workplace, including by email and at union meetings, for members to consider in their own time.

He said they were not, however, allowed to display union material in areas accessible to the public, nor election advertising anywhere on the premises.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders must be able to trust that the public service serves the government of the day with equal professionalism, regardless of political persuasion," Sir Brian wrote.

World.title: Government accepts all Covid-19 inquiry's recommendations 'in some form'
World.content:
Government to develop legislation to guide future pandemic responses Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

The government has accepted "in some form" all Covid-19 inquiry's recommendations, promising key advice will be made public within five working days in future pandemics.

The Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Covid 19 Response made 39 recommendations in its first "phase" and a further 24 recommendations in the second phase which focused primarily on how mandates were rolled out.

The final report was delivered in March, and the government has been considering its response since then.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said New Zealanders had placed enormous trust in the government and made real sacrifices to protect one another, and deserved "a clear account of what happened".

"This response is about learning from it."

Mixed reaction to government's response to Covid-19 inquiry Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

He said the government had accepted 21 recommendations in full, accepted 36 "in principle" and partially accepted the remaining six.

The resulting changes would be completed within 12 months where possible.

Cabinet had agreed to release advice behind any major decision affecting individuals' rights within five working days in future pandemics.

And while the government would not push ahead with standalone pandemic legislation, it would review the Health Act "to ensure any future response balances the protection of public health, the economy, and New Zealanders' rights".

Health Act review will take years - minister

Brown said the government's biggest undertaking now would be the Health Act review, which would go through a Select Committee process.

"We want to make sure that any legislation that is changed is done in a way that is transparent, that allows for people to make submissions," he said.

"Because we're balancing the economy with health and also people's rights and freedoms."

He expected the review would take several years.

Brow said he would be meeting with officials every three months to ensure they were acting on the inquiry's recommendations.

Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall said the government needed to put money behind its response, to make any difference.

"It's incredibly disappointing to see that the recommendations to strengthen the health system are all unfunded," she said.

"We're not going to have a different pandemic experience in the future unless public health systems are strengthened."

Deputy Prime Minister and ACT party leader David Seymour said the government decided against pandemic legislation because it did not need any more power.

"We're actually here to stand up for the rights of people to go to school, run their businesses, and not inherit $100 billion worth of extra debt, which is what happened last time."

New Zealand First's leader and fellow coalition partner Winston Peters said the government's response to the inquiry was "pathetic".

"We're going to make sure there's going to be another inquiry, so people who were maltreated and abused, and not given the right advice, do get some justice."

Green Party co-leader Chloe Swarbrick said the government was not adequately funding front line health staff.

"You have a government right now that has actively undermined the health system's capacity to actually respond to the next pandemic, that's incredibly concerning," she said.

World.title: Human Rights Commission warns Treaty clause overhaul increases legal uncertainty
World.content:
Human Rights Commission urges government to abandon laws that refer to Treaty clauses Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

The Human Rights Commission (HRC) is urging the government to scrap its planned amendment of Te Tiriti o Waitangi clauses, warning it could create more confusion and deepen division.

In a submission published on Tuesday, the Commission said the government's proposals were "constitutionally regressive" and risked weakening Treaty protections.

In May, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the coalition would change or remove references to the Treaty of Waitangi in 19 pieces of legislation "in the interests of increasing certainty and supporting compliance".

But HRC Indigenous Governance Partner Dayle Takitimu said it would have the opposite effect.

Human Rights Commission Indigenous Governance Partner Dayle Takitimu. Te Kāhui Tika Tangata Human Rights Commission

"The government said it wants clarity, but many Māori, legal experts, the Waitangi Tribunal, the Human Rights Commission, and international bodies say the review risks doing the opposite: weakening protections, reducing accountability, and increasing conflict.

"Achieving clarity - if that is the aim of the exercise - doesn't require watering down obligations to the bare minimum.

"Certainty and clarity are better achieved by following agreed human rights standards which support honouring treaties and respecting Indigenous peoples' human rights."

The Commission concluded that the government's plan downgraded Te Tiriti obligations and was "likely to increase, not reduce, uncertainty and litigation risk."

The changes risked intensifying racial tension and harming Crown-Māori relations, it said.

It also criticised the review, which recommended the changes, saying Māori had not been properly consulted throughout.

The review was secured by New Zealand First during coalition negotiations with National after the last election.

The Commission called on the government to abandon its changes and instead work with Māori on any replacement.

"Te Tiriti is not a side issue or a drafting inconvenience; it is part of the constitutional and human rights foundation of Aotearoa," Takitimu said.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In a statement, Goldsmith said the coalition did not agree or accept that its actions amount to "lowering the threshold of Treaty obligations".

In May, the government announced it would remove references to the Treaty principles in seven pieces of legislation.

Another 10 would be watered down, and two made "more specific".

At the time, Goldsmith said iwi would be consulted, and all New Zealanders could have their say through the select committee process.

"Over the last 30 or 40 years, Parliament has made all sorts of references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Sometimes it's 'honour', or 'have regard to', or 'give effect to', or 'take into account'," Goldsmith said.

World.title: Upper Hutt mayor: Don't force us to amalgamate with Wellington councils
World.content:
Upper Hutt's mayor is urging other Wellington councils not to force it into amalgamating against its will.

Councils across the motu have until August 9 to come up with plans to simplify local government, but in the capital there's still stark disagreement about the details.

The current proposal has Wellington, Upper Hutt, Lower Hutt, and Porirua city councils merging, as well as three Wairarapa councils and potentially Kāpiti District Council.

A layer of community councils would sit beneath that.

An email that Wellington Mayor Andrew Little sent last week to all councillors, which RNZ has seen, said Upper Hutt intended to vote against a plan to merge with the other Wellington councils.

The email said the city's mayor Peri Zee intended to ask councillors in each council to propose an amendment to have Upper Hutt excluded from any amalgamation proposal.

Zee told RNZ she was sceptical of amalgamation.

"I haven't yet heard anybody articulate the value proposition, or the outcomes we expect to get from this project.

"Our region already has strong regional governance in things like transport."

Upper Hutt mayor urging Wellington councils not to force amalgamation Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Analysis by consultants MartinJenkins showed a Wellington council made up of the city, Hutt Valley and Porirua councils could cost $290 million to set up and result in savings of $930 million over 25 years.

Zee said amalgamation would not deliver enough benefits for ratepayers.

She said she would ask elected members across the region to respect local decision-making if Upper Hutt votes against the idea next week.

"If a council votes no, that means no... and I would expect that they would respect that."

But that plea may be rejected.

Little said the proposal he would submit, if it was backed by his council, would include the region's four metro councils.

He said ministers had ultimately designed the process this way.

"Ministers can say it doesn't make sense for you not to be in it, therefore you're in it."

Little said he wants the Wellington region to decide it's own fate, and not leave the plan up to the Government by missing a deadline.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He believed the benefits, including savings, from a larger council would be a win for ratepayers in the long run.

"We're not setting up for a few years, we're setting up an arrangement that is intended to last for two or three decades."

A majority of 3016 surveyed Wellington city residents said they wanted councillors to forge ahead with merger plans.

About 85 percent said they supported councillors putting forward plans, with 68 percent strongly supporting that and 17 percent somewhat supporting that.

Little said councillors were still debating amalgamation. He expected a decision next week.

What Wellingtonians think of amalgamation

Resident Ellen Blake believed forced amalgamation jeopardised Wellington city's special character.

"We have lots of council housing, we've got significant nature restoration programmes, those are all unique to Wellington - and not to the rest of the region. So we've got our own local identity, and we want to keep it."

Climate consultant Matt Raeburn was more positive about the idea. On Wednesday he told councillors in the capital that merging would help the region address climate change.

He said in his opinion, Wellington's voice was currently weaker than Auckland council's unified one when it came to climate.

"From central governments over the last few years, and frankly even before that, the message to councils has increasingly been you're on your own.

World.title: Cash and property worth $800k seized from drug-selling Wairoa couple
World.content:
A Wairoa couple convicted of selling drugs stand to lose more than $800,000 worth of cash and assets - including six properties.

The Gisborne High Court ordered the forfeiture on Wednesday, which came after a long-running police investigation into Aria Hubbard and her partner Samson Edwards - a Mongrel Mob Barbarian Motorcycle Club member.

Acting Detective Sergeant Shaun Kennard said the pair was arrested in 2021 and convicted on charges of supplying and distributing methamphetamine in Wairoa.

He said the forfeiture of the couple's criminal proceeds included one commercial property, five residential properties, more than $150,000 in cash, five vehicles, a motorbike, jet ski and jewellery.

The investigation found the pair had deposited more than $200,000 into their bank account and spent almost $400,000 in cash, Kennard said.

"The cash was used to facilitate the purchases of vehicles, jewellery and residential property, as well as paying for renovations on the various properties they owned."

He said some of the property was under different names "in an apparent attempt to separate themselves from the offending and impact the efforts to identify and seize it".

Kennard warned businesses to be careful when accepting large cash payments from gang members to avoid unwittingly laundering money.

World.title: Benji Marshall denies claims of Tigers players vaping in gym
World.content:
Benji Marshall admits Wests Tigers need to address slipping club standards, but has refuted reports of players vaping in the NRL club's gymnasium.

The Tigers coach on Wednesday fronted the media to affirm his "love" for Adam Doueihi, almost a week after the 27-year-old disagreed with a move out of halfback and walked out on the club.

Media suggestions had been that aside from the positional switch, Doueihi was dismayed by a lack of professionalism and accountability at the struggling joint venture, which has not played finals since 2011.

Doueihi expected to return to Tigers training Adam Doueihi is expected to resume training with Wests Tigers on Tuesday after the playmaker underwent crisis talks with coach Benji Marshall and club officials.

The Tigers enter round 22 in 16th place on the ladder, despite sitting third earlier in the year and most recently suffering a 46-point loss to Canberra with their season on the line.

Marshall conceded the Tigers had work to do to improve their standards, but denied the club had a culture problem that contributed to their on-field struggles.

"I don't feel like there's a culture problem," he said.

"[But] if we're talking about standards and that, there's probably a few things we might've walked past recently that we need to address."

Marshall refuted media reports of a culture of vaping during gym sessions.

"I can tell you now that no-one's vaping in the gym. That's actually fabricated or misinformation," he said.

"Is there a vaping problem? Probably, with players, but with young men, you can't tell them whether they vape or smoke.

"I definitely can't control what they do 24/7. I'm not with them all the time."

Meanwhile, a remorseful Doueihi admits he can be "stubborn" and "a hard player to deal with", but insists he is committed to Wests Tigers following his highly publicised dummy spit.

Adam Doueihi cast the Tigers into the spotlight for all the wrong reasons. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

Doueihi conceded he should "definitely" have played the Tigers' must-win game against the Raiders last Saturday, rather than walk out after Marshall's decision to move him from halfback.

The 27-year-old said "miscommunication" had led to friction between he and Marshall, who had hoped to play him at lock against the Raiders.

"Benj knows I'd play front row for him. I never put myself above the team," he said.

"Was there a bit of communication breakdown there, and did I take it the wrong way? Yeah, and I'm happy to wear that."

The star utility was visibly emotional fronting a media scrum at Tigers headquarters on Wednesday, two days after crisis talks brought him back into the fold.

Doueihi said there were multiple factors that had led him to "lose [his] head" last week, including conversations with Marshall, the 16th-placed Tigers' disappointing season and a disruptive week that included a visit to the NRL judiciary.

The Tigers' season has fallen apart in recent weeks. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Those factors notwithstanding, Doueihi conceded he was to blame for bringing yet another off-field drama upon the sputtering joint venture.

"I know that at times, I can be a hard player to deal with," Doueihi said.

"I just put this stubborn head on that I have at times, and put this ego on that I have at times and just couldn't get myself in the right headspace to play. That's the reality of it.

"When you're fighting so hard and you have a big week and you go to the judiciary and you're not used to it, and you're losing, and you just want to see this club winning, add a bit of miscommunication, which I mentioned, to Benj.

"I'm an over-thinker and I love being well-prepared for stuff. You add that all together, and it just got the better of me last week."

AAP

World.title: Son of a gun Hewitt takes top-100 scalp in ATP first
World.content:
Cruz Hewitt's victory in his ATP Tour main-draw debut is set to rocket the son of a gun up the world rankings.

Fresh off a run to the Wimbledon boys final, Hewitt beat former world number 37 Marcus Giron — currently ranked 85 — 6-3, 6-4 in Washington DC on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

The Australian, who didn't face a break point, became the fourth man born in 2008 or later to win a tour-level match and the youngest Washington match-winner since Japan's Kei Nishikori in 2007.

The teen qualified thanks to walkovers after leading both Dusan Lajovic and top-seed Zach Svajda and has surged 255 places to number 357 in the ATP's live rankings.

He'll play the winner of countryman and mentor Alex de Minaur and former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas in the next round.

Cruz Hewitt's (right) win at the DC Open means he could face countryman Alex de Minaur next up in the round of 16. (Getty Images: Paul Morigi)

He had warmed up with father Lleyton, the former world number one, two-time major winner and 2004 Washington champion, who told him to lap up the moment.

"[He told me] mainly to enjoy it, because it was my first tour-level match … and to take every point one-by-one, to enjoy the atmosphere and to enjoy the crowd and that is what I did," he said.

Cruz said he was handling the pressure of carrying the Hewitt name "as best as I can".

"There is obviously a little bit of pressure, but I try to take the positives out of it as well, and I am happy with how I am dealing with it so far," he added.

"I am really happy with how I competed today. I came out and started pretty well, and I am thrilled to get through to the next round."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

De Minaur is defending his title in the American capital and fresh off a two-day Portofino honeymoon after marrying fellow pro Katie Boulter in Tuscany last month.

"It was an amazing time, everything we could have ever imagined," said De Minaur, who is coming off the disappointment of an upset fourth-round Wimbledon loss.

"It was like our own little movie. We were able to celebrate with family and friends and have a very small honeymoon.

"Then we're on a flight here to Washington and getting our heads screwed back on and back to being tennis players."

AAP

World.title: FIFA boss unveils $US20b plan to sell World Cup to Kushner consortium
World.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino's plan to create a $US20 billion ($29 billion) company running the World Cup with private investors, including the Kushner family, has been attacked by European football body UEFA.

"It is not FIFA's to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "None of us are the owners of football."

Mr Infantino's plans to form a commercial subsidiary, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup, were first reported by The Times of London.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

FIFA said in a statement FFE would raise up to $US4.2 billion later this year to help fund development programs "based on an initial equity valuation of $US20 billion by carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests".

FIFA is working with JP Morgan while intended investors include Thrive Eternal, launched by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

The men's World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Mr Trump and Mr Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties, including from UEFA.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially," UEFA said, responding to the reports of selling stakes in FIFA competitions.

FIFA is a Swiss-based not-for-profit association of its 211 national member federations worldwide.

The brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner (pictured), is among the potential World Cup investors. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

Those members must approve any plan and would get the chance "to access up to $US20 million in one-off capital", FIFA said.

"This is about the democratisation of football worldwide," Mr Infantino said in a FIFA statement, which added that "a consultation process has begun".

UEFA, however, said it took reports of the project "extremely seriously. So should every national Football Association".

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," said UEFA, which comprises 55 of the FIFA members.

FIFA emphasising financial benefits for members

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino has promised to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup. (Getty Images)

FIFA said Mr Infantino had detailed the outline of Tuesday's surprise announcement to members who met in Manhattan on July 18 ahead of the World Cup final.

There, Mr Infantino promised to "unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that FIFA has".

FIFA's statement emphasised how much money each of its 211 members could get in the "FIFA Fast-Forward Program", running until 2038.

Instead of the promised $US8 million each in development funds in the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, it would be $US20 million, then $US22 million and $US24 million in the following cycles.

FIFA banked record World Cup income of about $US12 billion from the 2026 tournament, which had unprecedentedly high prices for tickets and hospitality across the US, Canada and Mexico.

World Cup winners Spain will be one of six nations hosting matches at the 2030 World Cup.

It was unclear how that money could be matched from Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-hosting the 2030 men's edition.

Member federations could choose if they wanted to take part in the new financial opportunities, FIFA said.

"FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions," the soccer body said.

FIFA's integrity standards were called into question during the World Cup, including by team coaches, Norway's soccer federation and a top European public body, the Council of Europe.

FIFA's previous attempt to privatise assets

Infantino has built stronger ties with Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman throughout his tenure as FIFA boss. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Mr Infantino's 11-year FIFA presidency has become increasingly controversial, and this is the second time he has tried to push through a multi-billion-dollar deal with private backers.

In 2018 he proposed a secretive $US25 billion offer over 12 years with SoftBank of Japan to create new global competitions, including an expanded men's Club World Cup, seemingly backed by Saudi Arabian money.

That ultimately failed after meeting fierce resistance from UEFA, which saw threats to its prize assets: the Champions League and the European Championship.

Mr Infantino still built closer ties to Saudi soccer and the kingdom's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman. Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup, and largely funded the revamped men's Club World Cup hosted in the US last year.

What does this mean for Infantino's future?

The financial success of the just-ended World Cup has made it likely that Mr Infantino will be re-elected unopposed next year for a fourth and final term in office through to 2031.

At his re-election in 2023 in Rwanda, Mr Infantino suggested any CEO delivering similar financial results would be kept in the job forever.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Speculation has swirled for years that Mr Infantino might want a different global role in soccer beyond his FIFA presidency, which is due to end when he is 61.

The Times reported on Tuesday that a CEO-like commissioner role of the new FFE operation could be created for him.

"This has never been discussed," FIFA said in a statement on Wednesday (AEST). "However, the FIFA president and the FIFA administration will and must have leading roles in this entity — if approved."

There was no timetable suggested for debate and decisions by FIFA, its ruling Council chaired by Mr Infantino, and the 211 members.

FIFA is scheduled to hold an online congress on November 23 to confirm hosts of the Women's World Cup editions in 2031 and 2035.

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Record beaten five times in 10 minutes, pool haka thrills
World.content:
New Zealand swimmers pay tribute to a victorious teammate by performing the haka, a Pakistani lawn bowler fits in some work shifts and a weightlifting record falls a staggering five times.

Here are the quick hits from day five of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'Super proud' New Zealanders

Lewis Clareburt and his New Zealand teammates perform the haka after his victory. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

New Zealand swimmer Lewis Clareburt received a double honour after winning the men's 400-metre individual medley final.

Aside from being awarded the gold medal, Clareburt was the recipient of a haka proudly performed by his New Zealand teammates.

The Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd also appreciated the gesture.

"People really respect it [the haka] around the world and it makes me super proud to be a Kiwi," Clareburt told reporters.

The crowd erupted when the New Zealanders performed the haka. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Clareburt won the men's 200m butterfly earlier in the swimming program.

2. Lawn bowler works double shift

Mohammed Ayub Qureshi competing in the lawn bowls. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

No-one can accuse lawn bowler Mohammed Ayub Qureshi of not being a multitasker.

Qureshi competed for Pakistan in the men's singles event while also working at his restaurant in Glasgow.

Last Friday afternoon local time, he faced off against Scotland's Jason Banks before heading to the restaurant to work the evening rush.

Showing what the Commonwealth Games are all about, Qureshi invited Banks to drop by for a meal after the Scot sealed victory.

Loading Instagram content

"I was too scared before I played him in case he spiced up my food too much," Banks said.

It is the second time Qureshi has represented Pakistan at the Commonwealth Games in the city that has been his home for more than 50 years.

3. Record falls again and again

Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad ended a run of record-breaking lifts. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

What could possibly be better than seeing the Commonwealth record broken at a Commonwealth Games?

Well, seeing the same one be beaten five times in the space of 10 minutes or so would probably do it.

That is exactly what happened in the men's 88-kilogram weightlifting competition, with Cameron McTaggart, Braydon Kennedy and Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad all achieving new standards in rapid succession.

New Zealander McTaggart started things off with a 154kg lift.

That was swiftly bettered by Canada's Kennedy, who lifted 155kg with his first attempt.

McTaggart tried to better that, but missed at 157kg with his final snatch.

Then Malaysian lifter Muhammad entered the chat.

Neither he nor Kennedy could get 160kg up on their first attempts at the weight, but Muhammad did so on his second.

Then Kennedy threw up 161kg, so Muhammad added another kilo for the newest and final record of 162kg.

4. Aussies snare two golds in an hour

Breanna Scott won gold on the beam. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Breanna Scott already had a gold medal from this Commonwealth Games when she stepped out onto the balance beam on Tuesday.

After she flipped off it at the end of her routine, she had a second.

"It's pretty overwhelming to be honest, none of it has sunk in yet," she told Channel Seven after the final.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

She, and the rest of the Australian team, barely had time to let it, to be fair.

Jesse Moore delivered a superb routine to secure gold. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

An hour or so later, Australia had a second gold of the session.

Jesse Moore broke his duck to claim a sensational gold on the parallel bars.

His was Australia's ninth gymnastics medal of these Games.

5. Athlete on track twice in 34 minutes

Howard Tapuaiga Siila competing in the men's 800m heats. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Howard Tapuaiga Siila knew he had a full schedule on his hands when he arrived at the Scotstoun Stadium on day five.

The Tuvalu athlete was entered in both the men's 400m and 800m heats, which is a daunting task at the best of times.

But for Siila, there was only 34 minutes between the start of each race.

He took off in his 800m heat at 11:33am local time, finishing eighth in 2:32.38.

Siila was back on the track for the 400m at 12:07pm, finishing eighth via a time of 55.96.

Both were season-best times.

Competing in both events was planned, but there was one hitch.

"When I decided to enter the races we weren't sure of the scheduling," Siila told reporters in the mixed zone.

World.title: 'Biggest cheat in cricket history': Clicking scandal causes outrage
World.content:
An amateur cricket match in England has become a viral sensation after allegations of cheating were shared on social media.

A video, which claims to show a fielder clicking his fingers to imitate the sound of a bat connecting with the ball before a player is called out, has been viewed millions of times on X.

The poster of the video described it as "about the worst case of cheating I've ever seen in cricket".

Loading Instagram content

"First slip clicks his fingers to imitate an edge, bat nowhere near it and given out," the post read.

The video of a match involving North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League team Saltburn has been greeted with outrage online and generated headlines around the world.

TV presenter Piers Morgan weighed in, describing the player involved as the "biggest cheat in cricket history" and wondered how many batters' days "has he ruined?"

The league said in a statement on X that it had received a formal complaint regarding a game on Saturday, but did not reveal which teams were involved. However, it is understood the investigation is focused on the clicking.

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made," it said.

There was no immediate response when The Associated Press contacted the league and Saltburn for comment.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: 'The Aussies are on fire' on a night where that should've been impossible
World.content:
In the land of lochs, the announcer at Scotstoun Stadium couldn't figure out the first half of his name, but Lachlan Kennedy's performance on a sodden night in Glasgow ensured Australia will never forget it.

The weather on Tuesday night couldn't have been much more Scottish.

It was teeming basically all night, to the point the women's high jump final was halted for 45 minutes and the women's hammer throw probably should have been.

There were only two brief windows when the rain turned from a downpour to a drizzle, and it just so happened to be the moments "Lacklan" Kennedy was welcomed to the newly laid blue track.

The support crew was working overtime to make things vaguely manageable. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

It sounds like the sort of apocryphal tale told about Don Bradman in an era before the footage existed to prove your grandad was lying to you.

But it really happened.

To be clear, it wasn't dry, but no wetter than the night in March when he beat rising superstar Gout Gout in the 200m at the Maurie Plant Meet.

That established him once again as not just a fast runner, but a man capable of performing under the most intense pressure. A man plying his trade against a boy still figuring his out.

And Kennedy did it again on the biggest stage, winning Australia's first men's 100 metres medal at the Commonwealth Games with silver behind Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme on the second night of an athletics program that has been backed to deliver so much for Australia.

After not running a heat, Lachie Kennedy came straight out and made a statement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It's all about rising to the occasion. I'm a big believer in you've got to bring your best when it matters most," Kennedy said.

"That's what we've been training for all season. We've all been planning for this competition here and my coach has clearly outdone himself."

It seems extreme to say he obliterated the national record of Patrick Johnson by taking it from 9.93 down to 9.85, but 0.08 of a second means something different to folks like Kennedy than it does us mere mortals.

In the 58 years since Jim Hines broke the 10-second barrier in the 100 metres, only 232 more have people dipped into single digits.

Aussie sprinters storm to 100m medals Lachlan Kennedy and Torrie Lewis set new national records in claiming 100m medals, while a host of Australians take gold across athletics and swimming.

The margins are so fine in the jewel in the athletics crown that there have been 1,550 legal runs in 0.42 of a second between 10 flat and Usain Bolt's world record of 9.58.

Most are from the United States, Jamaica and spread across Africa, and just two from Australia, with Kennedy the only one since 2003.

Kennedy stands alone in some respects, but is proud to be part of a pack pushing each other towards greatness.

Gout's rise trained a spotlight on the team, whose performances with that attention have proved it warranted.

"Aussie track is clearly in the best spot it's ever been, our team is so strong … We're in a real golden age," Kennedy said.

That was clearly evident as Kennedy — after running alongside compatriot Eddie Nketia, who finished sixth in the final after laying down a PB of 10.03 in the semis — was still talking to the media in the mixed zone when Torrie Lewis won bronze in the women's final.

Loading...

"The Aussies are on fire," Kennedy said as he cheered Lewis on to the team's third of six medals on the night.

Lewis also set a new national record, but rather than breaking a record that had stood for 23 years, hers had barely stood for 23 hours.

Lewis's 10.99 in the women's final came after her 11 flat in the semi, which lowered her own record of 11.04 from a week prior.

All in an event she wasn't even sure she wanted to compete in.

Torrie Lewis followed Lachie Kennedy into the history books. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Lewis is a beneficiary of the controversial automatic qualifiers into the semis of her pet 200m event, where she'll be hoping for more silver (or better) ware before the relays kick off in the ultimate representation of what this team can do.

"I have a day off tomorrow, luckily with the bye, then Thursday see how I pull up for the semifinal and hopefully I can do something special there as well," she said.

Lewis and Kennedy were the headlines due to Australia's historic lack of truly exceptional flat sprint talent since the days of Raelene Boyle.

We've jumped at a few false dawns and sometimes athletes have been unable to live up to those expectations, while field sensations like Steve Hooker, Nina Kennedy, Eleanor Patterson, Matt Denny, Nicola Olyslagers and a cavalcade of women's javelin chuckers have been consistently brilliant.

The anachronisms of the Commonwealth The Commonwealth Games continues to roll on despite calls to decolonise our lives, with Scotland of all places a strange venue to stage two celebrations of the British Empire over the past 12 years.

They were again on Tuesday night: Patterson and Olyslagers went 1-2 to continue their impossibly consistent excellence in the high jump, and 22-year-old Lara Roberts broke through for her first major international medal.

Patterson said it was "phenomenal" to see the runners joining the jumpers and throwers in contention for medals.

"I was out there and you get to have a lay of the land and you understand what's going on," she said.

"I definitely took in my stride that there was a lot of Aussies there and seeing how well everyone was doing.

"Athletics in Australia, it's going off. I want the whole of Australia to know that we're taking it to the world, we're representing Australia very well and we're not bad, we're pretty bloody good."

Back on the track Ky Robinson kicked off the stunning hour and a half with victory in the 10,000m.

Australian athletics has had a number of these special nights of late, so much so that it risks becoming expected.

Australians have become so used to success in the pool that we have become somewhat blasé about the brilliance of our aquatic elite, but for now, on relatively dry land in Scotstoun there really is no other word for it.

That was special.

World.title: 'My time': Young gun Southam dethrones Chalmers in 100m final
World.content:
Kyle Chalmers has been dethroned as the Commonwealth Games 100m freestyle king in Glasgow, the "Big Tuna" having been reeled in by young friend and rival Flynn Southam in a landmark changing-of-the-guard moment.

With a potential record-breaking 10th Commonwealth gold in his sights, Chalmers had his proud record of never having been beaten by an Australian in major international competition dismantled by 21-year-old Southam in the Tollcross pool.

Southam's glory, fuelled by indignation at how he'd been somewhat dismissed as just a relay workhorse, set the tone for yet another medal-laden session of Dolphins' domination on the penultimate night of the program.

Jenna Forrester sealed her own golden treble in a remarkable breakthrough meet, adding a thrilling 200m individual medley triumph to the surprise 200m backstroke and 400m IM titles she'd already annexed.

And the night kicked off with 22-year-old Queenslander Kirralee Hayes taking the para gold medal in the 50m freestyle S13 final, and another Australian, Jenna Jones, taking bronze.

But Southam's win took pride of place, the young Fremantle-born, NSW-raised prospect finally fulfilling his potential as the most likely successor to "King Kyle", clocking a searing 47.13 seconds to bronze medallist Chalmers' 47.74. The pair were split by Welshman Matt Richards (47.64).

"Me and Kyle have utmost respect for one another. But it's my time to shine, and I know that," boomed Southam.

"I've been due for this, and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here as a little boy — but now I'm a man, and I belong here."

Flynn Southam says the Commonwealth Games are his breakout meet after winning gold in the men's 100m freestyle. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For Chalmers, though, cheered on by his wife, Norwegian international swimmer Ingeborg Loyning and baby daughter Astrid, there was a mixture of frustration that he couldn't land the 10th gold and 12th medal that would have taken him past the great Ian Thorpe as Australia's most successful men's swimmer ever at the Games.

Port Lincoln's 28-year-old maestro is likely to still have a chance, though, in the 50m butterfly final on the final day of competition in what could be his final appearance at the Games.

Admitting that he knew the passing-of-the-baton moment was inevitably coming at some point soon, Chalmers had hoped to delay it but was happy to tip his hat to the young gun after being the first to congratulate him.

"I'm completely fine with it," Chalmers said.

"I'd rather be in the race for that to happen than be retired and seeing them swim faster than maybe what… well, he hasn't quite got me just yet, but it's very close to what my best ever was.

"When we were able to sit in the medal presentation, I really said, 'You know, this is your moment. I'm so proud of you, enjoy your moment, enjoy singing the anthem.'

"I truly am so proud of him."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Southam had signalled his intentions at the start of the week when he clocked a sizzling lead-off relay leg of 47.09, which was just a hundredth of a second slower than Chalmers' all-time best and quicker than the South Australian star's 2026 best by half a second.

"It's pretty incredible. I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my success only comes from relays, and that's really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world," said Southam.

"Doubt always comes up, I was doubting myself as I was walking out, but it's about being able to turn that voice down and believing in yourself.

"I have Australia on my cap, I don't have just my name, so it's bigger than me."

Another medal came Australia's way with William Petric taking silver in the 400m individual medley behind New Zealand's double champion Lewis Clareburt.

AAP

World.title: 'Absolutely wild': Australian gymnasts top off Games with two more golds
World.content:
Breanna Scott and Jesse Moore have added to Australia's gold medal bonanza at the Commonwealth Games, taking out individual apparatus titles to finish their campaign in Glasgow.

Just minutes after Scott nailed a flashy balance beam routine to take out the title on her speciality apparatus, Moore hit every mark on the parallel bars to win another gold for Australia at Glasgow International Arena.

Scott scored 13.933 points for her routine, beating Singapore's Amanda Yap (13.233) and Lia-Monica Fontaine (13.00) of Canada.

Australian teammate and defending 2022 Birmingham champion Kate McDonald was last in eighth (12.166) after recovering from near-falls.

"[Balance beam] is definitely my favourite when it's going well," Scott said.

"It's kind of crazy, to be honest. It definitely hasn't sunk in yet.

"The last three days have just been absolutely wild.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

Scott wrapped up in Glasgow by winning her third medal and second gold medal.

She had contributed to Australia's dominant team all-around victory, before claiming silver in the women's individual all-around.

Backing up Scott, Moore found redemption on the parallel bars after missing the podium for the rings and pommel horse events.

Jesse Moore won his third gymnastics medal in Glasgow, winning gold in the men's parallel bars. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Australia's leading men's gymnast heading to Glasgow, Moore scored 14.000 points to pip Cypriot veteran Marios Georgiou (13.800 points) and Canada's Felix Dolci (13.300).

Scott and Moore's titles meant Australia medalled on every day of the five-day gymnastics competition in Glasgow.

Australia won nine medals, including four gold, behind Canada with 16 medals, seven of which were gold.

Moore said the gold medal was a weight off his shoulders.

"There's definitely been a bit of pressure building into these Commies with medal chances," Moore said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I knew I had one last crack to really have a go.

"This routine, I've done for years, so I could really trust myself and really go for it.

"I'm pretty stoked to get the gold."

The 23-year-old will leave the Games with three medals, having won a team bronze and an individual all-around bronze.

McDonald missed out on adding to her individual uneven bars gold and finished sixth in the floor routine final, ahead of 2022 Birmingham breakout star Georgia Godwin in seventh.

James Hardy settled for a fifth-placed finish on vault after claiming floor and rings bronze the day before, while 19-year-old Ritam Malik finished sixth on the parallel bars.

Australia's gymnastics medals

Gold (4): balance beam, uneven bars, team all-around (all women), parallel bars (men)

Silver (1): all-around (women)

Bronze (4): floor, rings, all-around, team all-around (all men)

AAP

Tech.title: The US is banning foreign robots
Tech.content:
The US government is targeting China with a new import ban on “advanced robotic devices” and power inverters made in foreign countries, as reported earlier by Reuters. In an announcement on Tuesday, the Federal Communications Commission says the ban will include “mobile” robots, such as humanoid and quadruped models — but it is not limited to robots that walk around.

China is also home to the world’s leading power inverter producers — Sungrow and the already-blacklisted Huawei — which are often used in solar panel arrays and other renewable energy systems. In its announcement, the FCC cites “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” as the reason for the ban.

A FAQ page published by the FCC defines an “advanced robotic device” as a machine that is capable of “locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground;” comes with a sensor that perceives the surrounding environment; and has a chip for network connectivity. It must also weigh more than 4.4 pounds (including its docking station, if it has one).

By that definition, even future robot vacuums would automatically be banned if they do not obtain a waiver. The FCC does not appear to be limiting this ban to robots with legs. In fact, the National Security Determination that the FCC is using to justify the move explicitly mentions The Verge’s reporting on the poor security of DJI’s Romo robovac.
